Hi [~accountid:712020:985a985c-b403-41bd-b116-abbf44b22175] , [~accountid:712020:726e5ea0-027c-4c31-a0fd-2c23b80dc56c] , [~accountid:712020:8bcb68bd-f8da-4da1-8320-2536f6bb0c0c] , some changes should be made to the contract before it can be signed. (I found out I don’t have Word on my computer yet so couldn’t change the contract directly, but for now I’ve summarized the changes below. I can upload a tracked-changes version as soon as I have Word installed. Then I’ll include the German version of the changes as well). 

+Fee (article 5)+: Leyton’s fee schedule doesn’t reflect the negotiated 7.15% average commission rate. A cap should be added to ensure this is the maximum effective rate:

* Notwithstanding the tiered fee schedule above, the aggregate remuneration payable to Leyton under this Agreement for all relevant financial years shall not exceed an effective blended commission rate of 7.15 % of the total research allowance granted to Bolt (exclusive of VAT).

+Duration (article 2(2)+: The current version prevents termination during the first four years and automatically renews every year unless cancelled. This should be replaced with something more flexible:

* This Agreement shall enter into force on the date of the last signature and shall remain in effect for an initial term of four (4) years (the ‘Initial Term’), unless terminated earlier in accordance with this Article.
* Either Party may terminate this Agreement for convenience at any time after the first anniversary of the Effective Date by giving the other Party thirty (30) days’ written notice.
* Either Party may terminate this Agreement with immediate effect by written notice if the other Party commits a material breach of its obligations under this Agreement and fails to remedy such breach within fourteen (14) days after receipt of a written notice requiring it to do so.
* This Agreement shall not renew automatically after expiry of the Initial Term; any extension shall require the express written agreement of both Parties.
* Termination shall be without prejudice to any rights or obligations accrued prior to the effective date of termination (including Leyton’s entitlement to remuneration for Services duly performed up to that date).”

+Invoicing (art. 6)+: Under the current wording, Leyton can bill Bolt before any tax credits have actually been approved - and Bolt only has 12 months to chase refunds if the application is rejected. Should be replaced with: 

* Leyton shall be entitled to invoice its remuneration only after the competent authority has issued a final decision granting the research allowance to Bolt. 
* If the application is rejected or partially rejected, Leyton shall not be entitled to any remuneration for the rejected portion. Any amounts already paid in advance shall be reimbursed within thirty (30) days after the rejection notice.
* By mutual agreement, Bolt may authorise an interim payment of up to 25 % of the estimated fee after submission of the complete application to the competent authority, provided that the remainder becomes due only upon approval of the research allowance.
* All invoices shall be payable within thirty (30) days of receipt of a correct and verifiable invoice.
* If any overpayment occurs due to later reductions, corrections or revocations of a grant decision, Leyton shall immediately refund the corresponding proportion of the fee to Bolt.
* Bolt shall not lose any rights to contest an invoice or to claim reimbursement because of time limits shorter than those under statutory law.

+Exclusivity (art. 7)+: Art. 7 currently prevents Bolt from using another service provider or self-file. This should be narrowed down to specific projects or the entire article deleted. 

Some other things that don’t necessarily need to be changed from a legal standpoint, but just flagging to make sure the necessary approvals are given:

* Liability (art. 8): Leyton’s liability is capped at the amount of their fee, which could potentially end up being very low. 
* Marketing rights (art. 3 (4)): Leyton can use Bolt’s name and logo in their marketing materials without prior consent. This can also be changed to require prior approval.

Hi [~accountid:712020:9c263122-6bc1-4bbe-91d7-c80d616c4514] please review below feedback from the local statutory auditor related to our proposal to sign the DPA. Please let me know your thoughts on the way forward. Best wishses, Karoli

_“We have now checked your request with our legal department and GDPR experts who advise numerous clients in the application of EU GDPR rules._

_Given your request, we ask for your understanding that_ *_we cannot and are not permitted_* _to sign the supplementary clause 16 (hereinafter referred to as clause) or the Data Processing Agreement (hereinafter referred to as DPA). Otherwise, I would violate professional CPA rules relating to independence of the auditor. Clause 16 is not necessary. It primarily stipulates that we are mutually obliged to comply with the applicable data protection regulations. Such an obligation already arises from the legal requirements (e.g., GDPR) and would only be declaratory. Regarding the alleged roles as controller (Bolt) and processor (nbs), we would like to point out that such a division of roles is not applicable in this case. According to Art. 4 No. 8 GDPR the processor processes the personal data on behalf of the controller. The key feature is that the_ *_processor processes personal data on the instructions of the controller_*_. This is not the case here._

_As auditors, we are required by law (see Section 43 of the German Audit Act)_ *_to be independent and act on our own responsibility_*_. When issuing audit reports and expert opinions, we are required to_ *_act impartially_*_. These legal regulations would be_ *_undermined if we were to perform our tasks in accordance with instructions_*_. This would be the case if we signed the DPA and adopted clause 16 in the proposed version. However, we can assure you that we comply with the applicable data protection regulations and take appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure compliance.”_

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Hi [~accountid:62567ec6a872710069210b83] , I have received the feedback from our external legal counsel and their recommendation would be to treat this contribution as an unconditional shareholders’ contribution that increases a company’s unrestricted equity. In this case will be required only a simple one-page document and board resolutions. Official corporate filings will be not required in this case, so this option would be much faster (and cheaper).

On the other hand, if we would like to increase the registered share capital of the entity it would require additional documentation and registration formalities with the Companies Registration Office. An increase in the registered share capital is normally not something that they recommend without there being any specific reason for it (e.g. if new shares are issued this would naturally have an impact on the share capital and in such case the registered share capital would increase).

Please let me know which option you would like to proceed with.

To clarify, I don’t think this setup involves any tax avoidance intent or an attempt by the ad agency to shift VAT to Bolt. In fact, VAT would be reverse-charged to the Czech ad agency from Bolt, given Bolt’s Estonian VAT registration. The ad agency would likely want a VAT invoice so that it can reclaim the VAT on the transaction. 

From my perspective, the key point is ensuring the arrangement reflects the *commercial reality*, which appears to be a *promotional credit* granted by the ad agency to Bolt for advertising services on their tablets. There’s no real need for a bilateral agreement if Bolt isn’t providing any reciprocal performance, data access, or licensing of the Bolt brand.

It’s not super clear to me how the ad agency will use the Bolt branding or why it needs this have this substantial IP right (which typically isn’t exchanged for discount credits). If the agency genuinely needs to use Bolt branding as part of a co-branded campaign (e.g., “Ads presented by Bolt” banner on all ads displayed on the tablet), that can be handled separately with specific brand-use approval. Otherwise, the cleanest and lowest-risk approach is to treat the credits as a *promotional incentive*, documented by the voucher itself or a simple confirmation letter, not a contract exchanging rights or services.

Hi [~accountid:712020:de758114-46c6-491b-85be-d23fd9c4b6ad] - thanks for your time on this morning’s call. To summarise the core points:

* We require opt-in consent to send direct marketing about third parties (including Shell) to drivers (i.e., the drivers must have selected ‘Partner offers’ in their consent preferences). We can only send such comms to drivers where we can practically argue that the comms are either: (a) not ‘direct’; or (b) not ‘marketing’ - this should be the focus when exploring options.
** (a) +Direct+ = Electronic comms targeted at specific drivers (e.g., Emails, SMS texts, social media messaging, push notifications, WhatsApp and +*Telegram*+ (on the understanding that ‘Telegram’ is electronic messaging))
** (b) +Marketing+ = Anything that promotes a service, product, offer or idea. EU regulators interpret this very broadly, and in the past regulators have interpreted this to include asking a person to consent to marketing (as has been proposed here).
* Our options are therefore as follows:
** ❌ *Option A*: Send emails to the drivers asking them to consent to receiving Shell marketing.
*** It is always open to the business to ignore our advice and proceed, provided that it is wiling to accept the compliance risks. Cyprus is a slightly lower risk jurisdiction than other EU countries from a marketing POV, and so there is a (low) chance that the regulator may not be interested in Bolt if we proceed on this basis. 
*** Nevertheless, the key risk here is that sending these emails without consent is very likely to be against local marketing laws, and so the regulator could take action against Bolt (which could mean financial penalties, enforcement notices etc.). As such, we would +*not*+ recommend this approach.
** ⚠️ *Option B*: Position the emails as not being ‘marketing’ (i.e., purely service communications).
*** Even if marketing forms part of a larger service message, the overall message will still be regarded as marketing (there are plenty of instances of previous cases/fines where this was the case). 
*** The only way to position the message as administrative, rather than promotional, would be to use an entirely neutral tone. This means: (i) not mentioning any third-party promotions at all; and (ii) not nudging drivers to ‘consent’ to marketing (instead, just flagging that they can change their preferences).
*** In practical terms, this would effectively be including the following sentence as part of a general update email: “_You can manage your communication preferences by going to [LINK]_”. This is an approach that the business could take, but I would +*not*+ recommend it, as it seems pointless - if we simply direct drivers to the marketing consents section of their app, they could actually _deselect_ further consents, which would undermine the whole point of the proposal.
** ✅ *Option C*: Position the marketing as not being ‘direct’.
*** Indirect means in this context would be in-app banners, pages on the driver portal and ‘just-in-time prompts’ (i.e., the driver visits the Shell Partner Offers page, and at that moment is asked if they would like to consent to receiving marketing materials).
*** As previously discussed, +*this is the most compliant approach and is the one I would ultimately recommend*+. Whenever I advise on promoting partner offers as part of Bolt Rewards, this is the approach I suggest where we do not have the relevant driver’s consent.
*** If this is completely unworkable for the business, then sending *push notifications* to the drivers is lower risk than sending them emails (as push notifications are less bothersome and so likely to result in drivers complaining to regulators) - however, this approach would still carry some risk as it still involves direct marketing - it therefore depends on how much risk the business is willing to accept 💡

* v4 metrics (non-time-slice):
** [Notebook|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/391991421278452?o=3829506390716583].
** Insights:
*** Average variance reduction is 28% compared to default metrics for non-rate metrics.
*** Average variance reduction is 12% compared to old CUPED for non-rate metrics.
*** Average variance reduction is <1% for rate metrics.
* v3 metrics (non-time-slice):
** [Notebook|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/1714503403610960?o=3829506390716583].
** Insights:
*** Variance reduction is 15-50% compared to default metrics for non-rate metrics.
*** For rate metrics, it is very hard to estimate, because capping is being done inconsistently. The correct approach is to cap numerator and denominator separately such that {{capped_metric = PERCENTILE(num, 0.99) / PERCENTILE(denom, 0.99)}}. However, it’s not always the case for v3 metrics as the ratio is often calculated as part of denormalized table (e.g., [search_order_ratio|https://github.com/bolteu/data-experimentation/blob/221dcb207125980dd9e1e9977d8caa979f0232a7/experimentation/experimentation/ab_processor/v3/metrics/targeting_user/rh/conversion/search_order_rate.yaml]) so we can only cap the final metric value. This is an incorrect approach!
*** *Rule of a thumb*: We can only cap additive metrics or metric components. (v4 suits here perfectly)
*** Given that in v3 a lot of metrics are non-additive, we cannot cap them consistently and provide accurate results.
*** Thus, together with [~accountid:6268ef8e429789006946b1ac] we decided to reject the capped CUPED implementation for v3 metrics.
* v3 metrics (time-slice):
** [Notebook|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/1234627500517475?o=3829506390716583].
** Insights:
*** Average variance reduction for metrics with high dispersion (gmv, profit) is 5-8% compared to old CUPED.
*** Average variance reduction for metrics with low dispersion (sessions, orders) is <1% compared to old CUPED.
**** Why is that? Because of user-block being an 1-2-hour window, so capping threshold for orders is 1 order.
*** The rejection reason for capped CUPED implementation is the same as for v3 non-time-slice metrics.

h2. Application Rules for Capping

# Apply capping to the _atomic, additive components_ of the metric, not to derived or composite expressions.
# For rate metrics, capping should be applied to the numerator and denominator separately before computing the rate.
# _(Needs further investigation)_ For more complex derived metrics (e.g., A * B / C), we need to cap each of the components separately before calculating the final expression.

        pl.col("month").cast(pl.Date).alias("month"),
        "city_name",
        "train_end_date",
        pl.col("forecast_start_date").cast(pl.Date).alias("forecast_start_date"),
        "finished_orders",
        "asp_local",
        "gmv_local",
    )
    .filter((pl.col("month") == pl.col("forecast_start_date")))
    .join(selected_scenarios, on=["month", "city_name"], how="inner")
    .join(
        actuals.select(
            "city_name",
            pl.col("month").cast(pl.Date).alias("month"),
            "finished_orders",
            "asp_local",
            "gmv_local",
        ),
        on=["city_name", "month"],
        how="left",
        suffix="_actual",
    )
)

METRIC_COLS = ["finished_orders", "asp_local", "gmv_local"]
ibm_with_actuals.with_columns(
    [
        (pl.col(col) - pl.col(col + "_actual")).alias(col + "_diff")
        for col in METRIC_COLS
    ]
).with_columns(
    [
        (pl.col(col + "_diff").abs() / pl.col(col + "_actual")).alias(col + "_mape")
        for col in METRIC_COLS
    ]
).with_columns(
    (pl.col("selected_scenario_label") == "SB").alias("was_sb_scenario_selected")
).group_by(
    "was_sb_scenario_selected"
).agg(
    *[
        pl.col(col + "_mape").mean().alias("mean_" + col + "_mape")
        for col in METRIC_COLS
    ],
    pl.col("city_name").count().alias("n_observations")
){noformat}

Hey, see my comments 🙂 

* The legal obligation cited (via § 46(2) OWiG) is not sufficient alone to assert that the authority has a direct right to demand the data from Bolt.
** This provision states that the authority tasked with prosecution in a administrative offence case has the same rights and obligations as the public prosecutor’s office in criminal proceedings, unless OWiG provides otherwise.
* Unless the letter or order cites a specific law or regulation beyond § 46 OWiG (for example a regional law or regulation on traffic enforcement, or a formal administrative information order under a statute) that obliges companies to provide data, Bolt would not have an unconditional data sharing obligation under that provision.
* Therefore, we should ask the authority for the specific legal basis for their request (e.g., municipal/NRW law, or an official order citing a law).
* In short, by itself, this is not a valid basis.

In Slovakia we have commission netting.

_Through commission netting, your campaigns/bonuses/compensations are reflected as a discount from your commission, instead of each having their individual invoices. Simply, your commission is reduced in the amount of your campaigns/bonuses/compensations - ensuring a more clear invoicing process, and less invoicing noise._

_For example, previously you would see a commission of 416.91€ and separate bonus lines of 11€ on your invoice, which totaled up to 361.92€. Now, you would only see a single row of commission in the amount of 361.92€, meaning the calculation is already done in the background._

Thanks [~accountid:712020:e6db7bf1-81f8-43b5-b50b-2b4bb57ce924] - coming back to you on the Driver ID point:

* It is correct that driver ID and partner ID are only visible to Bolt. As previously mentioned, the reason for this (i.e., why we generally only make these IDs visible _internally_, and not _externally_ to users) is for +*data security*+ reasons (i.e., if a malicious actor got hold of a driver’s account ID, they could use this to identify a driver’s data if the account’s contents were leaked as part of a data breach - Bolt has been subject to a few data breaches recently, and so this is always a risk). If we published the driver IDs on the leaderboard, then these would be publicly available (even if the public did not have _immediate_ means of linking each ID to a specific account), and so this raises security risks.
* I appreciate that we adopted the account ID approach in Germany last year. However, I would note the following:
** (1) On the SD ticket for Germany, the original advice given was to +_not_+ use driver IDs in the leaderboard, but to instead use a token. Ultimately, use of the driver ID was a _concession_, rather than the headline advice from my team.
** (2) Germany was one country where the total risk was overall lower (hence why we conceded to using driver IDs in that case). As we start to role this out in more countries, the security risk profile becomes higher, and so it would be sensible to adopt an approach that is sustainable (from a security POV) going forward - otherwise the more times we adopt this approach, the higher the security stakes become.
* The +*token*+ you suggest would certainly be a more compliant approach from my POV - it does not raise any account security concerns, and would achieve the same leaderboard end goals 🙂 

It is open to the business to nevertheless proceed with using driver IDs (as I appreciate there is engineering work that would be needed with the token), but as I say this raises security risks. Happy to discuss this further if you have any additional Qs

Similar setup we have with changes in VAT rate (from other countries, not PT), e.g. during a month N the VAT rate was 20%, in the month N + 1 → 25%; we issue invoice in the 3rd of month N+1 with the 20% VAT.

To reiterate, in the current setup it’s technically impossible to reissue the invoice with changes in the unique Billing identifiers, especially in the strict fiscal markets, such as Portugal. Bolt Business Account with new Billing Details have to be created for invoices to be issued correctly by the system.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt is testing a new category - ‘Meet & Greet’ - at Heathrow Airport ([RFC|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uzsNPLiC6GtuuDKWnq32944AM4L_C3hbgVEkqwstYWg/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.vlgvtdximz4s]).
** Service enables drivers to meet passengers inside the terminal (easier for passengers, and drivers compensated for additional time).
** Available to Bolt Business clients and a limited number of enrolled drivers (c. 523 in total - 1.2% of London driver pool). New category will be created under the ‘Business’ group for the pilot.
*** Only invited drivers will have access to the category - see email [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uzsNPLiC6GtuuDKWnq32944AM4L_C3hbgVEkqwstYWg/edit?tab=t.0]. Drivers opt-in by clicking a link.
** Rides will be scheduled (as scheduled rides) via ridebooker from the airport (business accounts).
*** Proposal to enroll ‘WeKnow’ as Heathrow client.
*** Once passenger has booked via ridebooker, they will have included their name / flight number in the ‘Add a note to the Drivers’ field.
*** Driver will receive passenger details and special notes (e.g., terminal, flight number, signage name) in an in-app chat.
** Drivers will display the passenger’s name in the terminal for identification.
*** Drivers will be issued with guidance on professionalism when greeting the passenger.
* Regional Legal has already advised the following:
** There is a reclass risk. Way around this is to make it optional (and to make professionalism guide optional).
** We should only be sharing strictly necessary passenger data (name and terminal - not full flight history). We should also advise drivers not to store or misuse passenger details.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Risk profile = {color:#36b37e}*Low*{color}.
** Nothing here suggests risk of bias, significant effect, sensitive data, security or tracking. As such, no DPIA needed.
** However, worth checking if we will be checking the driver’s location when in the airport (on foot) this may be intrusive.
* Transparency:
** Drivers = Already covered in the privacy notice. Only ‘new’ thing here is the data category.
*** Purpose = To enable and customise transportation services / To calculate prices (nothing new here).
*** Legal bases = Contractual necessity and Legitimate Interest.
** Passengers = New categories of data are flight details - these are not covered in the PN.
*** Nevertheless, purposes and legal bases are effectively the same (see above).
*** It would be interesting to know whether / how Bolt is retaining the flight details.
* Data Sharing:
** Worth digging into whether we will be sharing data with WeKnow / third party. If so, an agreement would be helpful.
* Marketing:
** We can likely rely on the soft opt-in exception here, as this is a new category and so it is ‘similar’ services ✅ 

||*Issue*||*Priority*||*Mitigations*||
|*Data Minimisation*
We should not be oversharing data about passenger flights with drivers, particularly as it is something we do not ordinarily process.|:orange_circle:|Only share details about the flights that the driver strictly needs to find the passenger (e.g., name, terminal, time, flight number).|
|*Transparency*
Our passenger privacy notice does not _explicitly_ currently cover sharing flight information with drivers. As such, there is a transparency gap - in particular, we should make clear what flight details will be shared with the driver (although the risk here is low, as it should be clear to the passenger as they provide it voluntarily).|:orange_circle:|Include the following disclaimer language on the same page as the ‘Add a note to the driver’s field':
* “_The information that you provide here will be shared with the driver for the purpose of navigating your pick-up. Bolt shares such information based on its legitimate interest in enabling transportation services by collecting passengers with drivers. For further information, see our privacy notice available at_ [_https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides_|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides]”
Alternatively, we could argue it is covered as UGC / App Usage Data, but none of these approaches are perfect.|
|*Disclosure of Passenger Data*
The driver will be displaying the passenger’s name publicly in the airport. Although low risk, we should ensure the data is not being over-disclosed.|:green_circle:|Per [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C073BV470P4/p1760958830861359], we should advise that only _first name + first letter of surname_ is shared.|
|*Data Sharing*
It is unclear whether we will be contracting with a third party here / sharing data. If so, we should ensure a proper agreement is implemented.|:green_circle:|Check with stakeholders whether we will be contracting with a third party here. If we are, consider processing roles and prepare an agreement.|
|*Live Location Tracking*
It is unclear whether we will be monitoring the driver’s location while they are on foot in the airport. If we are, this may be regarded as intrusive, and so may require additional review.|:green_circle:|Check with stakeholders whether we will be live location tracking. If we will:
* We can rely on legitimate interest to track their movements and argue that it is proportionate (as it is still technically an active trip, and so we would be tracking location anyway) - a +*LIA*+ would definitely be helpful though.
* We can argue it is covered by the privacy notice, however it may be worth +*making clear to drivers*+ that their presence in the airport will still be part of the active trip.|
|*DSRRs / Data Retention*
It is unclear whether we will be retaining details of passenger flights on our systems, once the passenger provides them during the flow.|:green_circle:|Advise that if we need to retain this information, we should do so clearly and in a way that is easily sourceable, as well as for no longer than is necessary. Otherwise, we should delete it.|

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Will we be contracting / sharing data with any third parties here?
** Will we be tracking the driver’s location even when they are in the airport on foot?
** How will we be retaining flight information on our systems?

Key takeaways from the meeting with the team:

* *Benefits vs. Penalties:* suggested that benefits are easier to handle from a legal and privacy standpoint compared to penalties. Penalties are seen as more complex due to potential interference with core service aspects like pricing and access to vehicles, and a higher risk of being perceived as discriminatory.
* *Transparency and Automated Decision-Making (ADM):* emphasised the importance of transparency in how driving behaviour affects the score to soften the risk associated with automated decision-making. Providing clear information on point deductions and planned incentives/penalties, along with a fallback for manual review, can help mitigate regulatory concerns.
* *Redress Mechanism:* proposed a semi-compliant approach to ADM by having a redress mechanism where users can dispute their score or penalties after it applies to the account. This would involve a manual review process, potentially through customer support, to confirm the score and penalty.
* *Iterative Approach:* There was agreement on taking a gradual and iterative approach to testing and rolling out both benefits and penalties, starting with benefits first due to their greater flexibility and lower associated risks and maintenance.
* *Stakeholder Management:* The team needs to prioritise and "sell" the benefits-first approach to stakeholders who may have different opinions, especially those focused on the harm dangerous users pose.
* *Customer Support:* Currently, customer support agents can revoke driving scores post-penalty assignment, but they don't fully understand how the driving score works and need to escalate cases to technical support for review.

Next actions:

* Team will discuss the preferred approach. Privacy assessments (PPRA, DPIA if needed, LIA) will follow once setup is agreed.

Meeting today with Eldar and Lev to discuss the benefits and penalties approach. Summary shared after the call on Slack (link to thread [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07K9SHJPJ7/p1760699954441209|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07K9SHJPJ7/p1760699954441209|smart-link] ):

_As just discussed with_ [_@eldar.nasyrov_|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U029SBRFP5K] _and_ [_@lev.goffert_|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U05G55B6Y5B]_, my overall feeling is that we should first focus on benefits and move to penalties once we have higher confidence in the scoring criteria, CS/operational robustness and user/public perception. Main reasons being that penalties:_

* _Move the feature closer to core service differentiation/restriction based on user profile (access to vehicles, pricing, liability) rather than a reward programme, which is more straightforward from a legal standpoint._
* _Carry a higher risk of being perceived as unfair treatment._
* _Require deeper country-by-country legal review (e.g., consumer law requirements, transportation/mobility law restrictions)._
* _Likely require amendments to country T&Cs and introduction of details about when and how penalties apply._
* _Offer less flexibility for iterative adjustment. If we change penalties or the logic (score criteria or thresholds), we may need to revise T&Cs, re-run legal reviews, communicate to users and introduce transitional arrangements._

_We might be able to frame certain penalties as upside benefits for high scorers, but we would need to assess them individually._

As a general principle, Bolt’s role as a platform is limited to ensuring compliance with our platform terms and conditions and applicable laws. *Any employment or contractual relationship, including disputes, between a Fleet Owner (FO) and a Driver is managed directly between those two parties*.

That said, Bolt may take action if the Driver’s behaviour violates our platform rules or safety standards - for example, harassment, threats, or fraudulent activity. In such cases, suspension or deactivation can be considered based on conduct observed or reported on the platform (e.g., communication via Bolt systems, safety risks, or policy breaches).

In this case, as long as the harassment is occurring directly toward the FO in a personal or external capacity, and not through the platform, it remains a matter between the FO and the Driver. However, if there’s evidence that the Driver is harassing or threatening anyone through Bolt’s systems, please escalate it directly.

{color:red}*Sergei Jakovlev [wrote|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C01PT0B6D70/p1761053428908069]*{color}:
Hi! There is a subtle difference:
• uses DB time
• various  use node time for block status
This is important when handling block events because events may come out of order and might show an outdated status, e.g. list a "completed block as active if the node time is a bit behind DB time, basically leading to incorrect logic for block that started and immediately ended.

Now, specifically in this case, "aborted" event is always going to be the final event for the block (it cannot be "re-started"), and, in addition to that, aborting a block uses an explicit flag, so the all methods should return the same state in particular for aborted blocks. The problem would be for naturally ending blocks, as they can still be listed as active in results of  call for *all* events, even if all blocks are actually ending. If blocks are always infinite and are always aborted (newer expiring normally), then that would not happen, but I think those blocks can expire, so this can lead to inconsistent state.

Please note that the issue exists for "started" and "completed" events as well - if a block is started and ended almost simultaneously, you can get events in any order, and  after the last event is handled will not necessarily produce the final block state.

Thanks [~accountid:61fd40abc224b80069c9d6cf] - I have taken a look from a privacy POV and my thoughts on your points are as follows:

* *Only sharing necessary information*: Agreed ✅  We should only be sharing passenger flight information that is +_strictly necessary_+ with the driver (i.e., the minimal amount of data needed to locate the passenger at the terminal - first name and +_first initial_+ of surname, terminal, flight time, perhaps flight number as well in case the flight is delayed and the driver needs to check this) 💡 
** NB. If the passenger is providing such data in a text box (i.e., we do not directly control exactly what data we are collecting), then this is ok as it is addressed by my disclaimer recommendation below.
* *Privacy notices*: It seems that the only ‘new’ data we are processing here is flight information - is that correct? If so, such data processing is +not+ covered in our privacy notices, and so there would be a transparency gap here ⚠️ To address this gap (and to mitigate the risk of passenger complaints to Bolt), I recommend including the following disclaimer language on the same page as the passenger enters their flight details (i.e., the ‘Add a note to the Drivers’ field) 💡 
** “_The information that you provide here will be shared with the driver for the purpose of navigating your pick-up. Bolt shares such information based on its legitimate interest in enabling transportation services by collecting passengers with drivers. For further information, see our privacy notice available at_ [+_https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides_+|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides]”
* *Driver reminders*: Fine with this approach ✅ 

----

I also have some other more general recommendations on this initiative from a privacy POV - please could someone comment on my questions here?

* *WeKnow data sharing*: Are we entering into an agreement with WeKnow (or a similar third party) that will involve user data sharing? (?) 
** If so then please let me know and I would be happy to review the agreement / recommend data sharing provisions 💡 
* *Driver location tracking*: Just to confirm - when a driver gets out of the car to meet the passenger in the terminal, I assume that we will continue to track their location via the Bolt app while they are ‘on foot’? (?) 
** If so then this is something that we can do (indeed, it makes sense as it is still an active trip), but we should consider additional precautions given that some drivers may view this kind of tracking as invasive. In particular, it would be worth including a sentence or two somewhere in the driver flow flagging that this will happen - I would be happy to prepare this if needed 💡 
* *Retention of flight information*: Will we be retaining the flight information provided by passengers on our systems? If so, for what purpose(s)? (?) 
** My advice on this is that we should only be keeping this on our systems if we strictly need it. If we do, we should make sure it is easily accessible in Admin to Bolt employees upon request (e.g., if the passenger makes a data request for this information) 💡

Hi [~accountid:712020:3d2dfcb9-5b90-4b13-a4e2-9b7530e3d83f], this is an example of a money claim against us (i.e. a civil procedure against us usually for a fixed amount, which we can either defend, mediate or settle outside of the formal claim). +If we don’t respond, we can be issued with a default judgment which we of course want to avoid.+ 

Here’s a previous money claim example which gives you an indication of the steps to follow (in this case we ended up mediating the claim) - [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-47366|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-47366|smart-link]. You’ll be able to see [~accountid:63fe21787c30bbd6b33e09d3]'s defence that she drafted which will be a good source for you in any event.  

I’d recommend following the steps in the ticket linked above, however in all money claims I’ve seen to date, the steps generally are as follows: 

* access the hyperlink set out in the letter, enter the claim number/given code, create an account (use the Legal team email address and, once created, put the log-in details on an *internal comment* on this ticket incase someone else in the team needs to log in). 
* review the claim details on the money claims portal.   
* loop in Jason, Britta, Ramone etc into this ticket so that they are aware of this claim. 
* summarise the facts of the claim on this ticket and attach any relevant documents to the ticket (i.e. the claim form/particulars of claim).
* ask follow-up questions for Britta/Ramone re details of the alleged claim. 
* once internal details are received, consider what our options/next steps may be (i.e. can we reasonably defend the claim?). Our ideal starting position would be to defend. 
* set out your initial thoughts/recommendation to Jason for approval. 
* draft a defence if applicable. 
* if you suggest settling the matter with the claimant directly (i.e. outside of the money claim portal), consider what sums to offer the claimant - [here’s an example of a money claim that we |https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-53365][*settled* |https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-53365][directly with the claimant|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-53365]. 
* set yourself calendar reminders for any deadlines (deadline to respond to the claim, deadline to make any payment to the claimant) etc. 
* add this as an item for your catch-ups with Jason. 
* update the claims tracker and the monthly TfL report once it’s circulated. 

Thank you!

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt has been approached by AdsGo (ads company in Czech Republic), who wants to install tablets in Bolt (fleet) cars that will display ads during rides. 
** Bolt does not own the fleets - these are owned by the fleet owners. AdsGo has already been negotiating with fleet owners separately (main cooperation would be between the ads company and the fleet owners).
*** NB. Seems unlikely that AdsGo would need Bolt’s approval to do this, since we don’t won the cars. But we are taking advantage of an opportunity.
** Nevertheless, Bolt wants to have a separate (direct) agreement with AdsGo, covering ad content, IP protection, right to remove the tablets and to formalise the offer terms (since AdsGo is generating income through our platform, they will be paying Bolt advertising credits).
*** Regional Legal is currently redrafting the agreement (expected on 22.10): “_Bolt is referring the ad agency to its network of drivers / facilitating sales and earn something in exchange for that referral rather than handing over it its proprietary data and branding rights to the ad agency_”
** Plan is to start the partnership at the beginning of November (I was only looped in on 21 October). This is going ahead regardless.
* Regional Legal has already flagged reclass risks with this approach (i.e., we cannot intervene with every single piece of ad content (beyond branding)).
* Under the arrangement, Bolt will grant AdsGo access to our user database (fleets and drivers, not riders).

+*ANALYSIS*+

* *Data Sharing*:
** It is currently unclear whether we are sharing any driver/FO data with AdsGo. If we are, we should implement a data sharing agreement. If not, then this is not an issue.
* *Marketing*:
** This does not appear to be targeted / direct marketing (and in any event, Bolt has little to no control over it). As such, this does not appear to be an issue.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** What data will the ads company have access to, and why does it need it / what will it do with it?
* Depending on whether any data sharing is happening here, we may need a DSA. If not, then I have no comments from a privacy POV ✅ 
** Our preference would be not to unless we strictly need to.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* General:
** It is not fully clear to me whether we will be _sharing_ personal data with AON here.
** These terms seem to be standard (present on the website). Very unlikely we can change them.
* Data Protection Schedule:
** Parties are characterised as independent controllers (this makes sense, as AON has a wide discretion here). Fine.
** Parties must comply with applicable privacy laws. Fine.
** Purposes (2.4) = Delivery of services, general correspondence with Bolt, screening of individuals associated with Bolt against sanctioned parties lists, and market research (after anonymisation). Fine.
** Retention (2.8) AON may retain data to meet legal obligations and defend legal claims. Fine.
** SCCs and UK IDTA are incorporated. Fine.
** However, the DSA is missing some of our standard protections ⚠️ 
*** Limited visibility of T/O measures (AON has a “_global data governance framework_” covering this, but we/InfoSec have not seen this), althugh likely to be robust.
*** PDBs must be notified without undue delay (not within 48 hours), although this is a minor point.
*** No explicit audit rights re privacy compliance.
*** No pro-Bolt indemnity for data privacy violations - this is important.
* Details of Processing (Appendix 1):
** Services are pensions consultancy services, commercial risk solutions, human capital solutions and health solutions.
** Types of data include health data, criminal records checks, racial data, images of ID cards, sexual orientation, tax code ⚠️ 
* General T&Cs:
** Bolt must make available to AON all docs that AON needs to execute the services.
** “_Transfer, storage, or processing of personal data by third parties shall take place only with the Client’s written consent_” - Fine, although there is a carve-out for third parties whose involvement is “_necessary_” for providing the services. In principle this is fine, due to C-C relationship, but it would be preferable for AON to seek approval for processors ⚠️ 
** (5.4) If consent is required for transferring personal data to AON, Bolt must forward such consent to AON ⚠️ 
** (8.2) AON liable for 4m CHF in cases of minor negligence. However, no privacy indemnity ⚠️ 

+*NEXT STEPS*+

** Will we actually be _sharing_ any personal data with AON here? If so, why?
** Do we have any scope for actually amending the agreement?
* If we are not actually sharing the data here, then this limits the risk profile substantially.
** If we are, we need to be careful re sharing A9/A10 data. We would also want to include indemnity provisions, processor authorisation and audit rights in the agreement.
* Check with the business whether there is any scope for suggesting edits. If there is, suggest them. If there is not, advise on the risks.

Hi [~accountid:712020:1d5390cd-af56-43c8-9d12-f431b20183ba], thank you for preparing the draft! I appreciate that you’re focusing on the key strategic points to keep discussions with Westminster moving. From a Legal perspective, that approach makes sense, however we would always recommend limiting our liability exposure as far as possible. 

As drafted (and as flagged above) the agreement currently gives the Council a broad indemnity (covering losses “whether or not the Council has been negligent”) and sets a liability cap of *£10 million*, while the insurance clause only requires *£5 million* cover which is disproportionate to the contract value and our standard liability position. 

To mitigate that, we’d recommend adding a short line into your draft (see draft below):

_“Clause 17 and 19: For completeness, we would also propose aligning the liability and indemnity provisions to ensure they remain proportionate and consistent with the insurance requirements under the agreement. Specifically, we suggest limiting the indemnity to losses arising from the Bolt’s own negligence or breach, removing clause 17.4 in its entirety and capping aggregate liability at a lower figure reflective of the contract value, rather than the £10 million currently stated.”_ 

Additionally, as already flagged, the agreement currently allows the Council to terminate or vary the agreement on 30 days' notice if any law, policy or regulation changes. This is highly discretionary and would allow them to terminate even if the change is minor or purely policy-driven. Do let me know if you would like me to draft some suggested wording to the Council to see whether there is scope to amend/clarify this point. 

Of course, this is ultimately a business decision depending on how sensitive timing is and how much pushback we expect from the Council, but from a Legal perspective we’d strongly recommend trying to narrow the exposure before signature.

Best wishes

Thank you for sharing the draft agreement. We appreciate the opportunity to review it and would like to propose a small number of amendments to ensure clarity and proportionality, given the one-year duration of the contract and our need to launch operations swiftly.

Suggested Amendments
Clause 4.3(b)
 We propose removing the requirement that “the Operator must always have a minimum of 50% of the permitted maximum fleet deployed in each Operational Zone at the beginning of each day (0600 hours)”.
 There is no clear operational justification for setting a minimum daily deployment threshold, particularly given the already high density of available bikes in the borough. Removing this requirement would enable more flexible and demand-responsive fleet management.

Clause 5 (Charges)
 We recommend structuring the annual charge per bike in proportion to the utilisation rate (e.g. 1 RPV = £135 per bike; 2 RPV = £275 per bike; 3 RPV = £410 per bike, and so on).
 This approach would link revenue to service usage and ensure that operators with smaller fleets or lower ride-per-vehicle rates are not disadvantaged compared with those operating at higher scale. It would also align incentives between operators and the Council.

Clause 17 and 19: For completeness, we would also propose aligning the liability and indemnity provisions to ensure they remain proportionate and consistent with the insurance requirements under the agreement. Specifically, we suggest limiting the indemnity to losses arising from the Bolt’s own negligence or breach, removing clause 17.4 in its entirety and capping aggregate liability at a lower figure reflective of the contract value, rather than the £10 million currently stated.

Clarifications Requested
Clause 4.3(c): Could you please clarify how the “maximum permitted fleet size in each Operational Zone” is defined?
Clause 5: The text refers to both a £275 fee per permitted bike and a £275 per bike per annum exceedance fee. If both rates are equivalent, what is the practical purpose of the fleet cap?
Timelines: Could you please confirm the anticipated timeline to finalise and sign the agreement?

Thank you again for your collaboration and responsiveness. We look forward to progressing to signature as soon as possible.

Kind regards,

    part_df = part_df[['id','item_code','report_id','quantity']].withColumnRenamed('id', 'part_id')

    city_df = dbt.source("ng_public_spark", "admin_system_city")
    city_df = city_df[['id','name','country_code']].withColumnRenamed('id', 'city_id')

    country_df = dbt.source("ng_public_spark", "admin_system_country")
    country_df = country_df[['code','name']].withColumnRenamed('code', 'country_code')

    open_reports_df = (part_df
                      .join(report_df, part_df.report_id == report_df.report_id, 'inner')
                      .join(city_df, report_df.city_id == city_df.city_id, 'inner')
                      .join(country_df, city_df.country_code == country_df.country_code, 'inner')
                      .filter(report_df.closed.isNull())
                      .select(
                          part_df.part_id,
                          part_df.item_code,
                          part_df.report_id,
                          part_df.quantity,
                          report_df.city_id,
                          report_df.entity_id.alias('vehicle_id'),
                          report_df.created,
                          report_df.closed,
                          city_df.name.alias('city_name'),
                          country_df.name.alias('country_name')
                      ))

    # Convert to pandas for the grouping logic (similar to notebook)
    df = open_reports_df.toPandas()
    
    # Group scooters by count of parts they wait for
    df_by_scooters = (pd.pivot_table(data=df,
                                    index='vehicle_id', 
                                    values=['quantity'], 
                                    aggfunc={'quantity':'sum'})
                     .reset_index()
                     .rename(columns={'quantity':'total_missing_part_for_this_scooter'}))

    # Merge back and sort
    df = df.merge(df_by_scooters, how='left', on='vehicle_id')
    df = df.sort_values(by='total_missing_part_for_this_scooter', ascending=True).reset_index(drop=True)
    df = df.dropna()

    #read rental fleet city area to join warehouse ids and city_ids
    area = dbt.source("ng_rental_spark", "rental_fleet_city_area")
    area = area.filter(area.type == 'warehouse')
    area = area[['workday_inventory_location_id','city_id']].withColumnRenamed('workday_inventory_location_id', 'location_id')

    # read inventory table
    balance = dbt.source("ng_rental_spark", "rental_workday_inventory_site_balance_daily")
    balance = balance.filter(balance.date_date == current_date())
    balance = balance[['company_id','location_id','purchase_item_id','quantity_available','location_name']]
    balance = balance.join(area, balance.location_id == area.location_id, 'left').select(
        balance.company_id,
        balance.location_id,
        balance.purchase_item_id,
        balance.quantity_available,
        balance.location_name,
        area.city_id
    )
    balance = balance.toPandas()

    df_out = pd.DataFrame(columns=['country','city','all_waiting_for_parts','actually_waiting_for_parts'])
    
    #Greedy algorythm
    #We go scooter by scooter, starting from scooters that wait for 1 part
    #In case part is found in the WH - we reduce available amount of parts by 1 and close report

    k=0

    for c in list(df.city_id.unique()):
        print(c)
        df_city=df[df['city_id']==c].reset_index(drop=True)
        balance_city = balance[balance['city_id']==c].reset_index(drop=True)
        for i in range(len(df_city)):
           for j in range(len(balance_city)): 
                if (df_city.at[i,'city_id']==balance_city.at[j,'city_id'])&(df_city.at[i,'item_code']==balance_city.at[j,'reference_id'])&(df_city.at[i,'quantity']<balance_city.at[j,'available_to_use']):
                    balance_city.at[j,'available_to_use']=balance_city.at[j,'available_to_use']-df_city.at[i,'quantity']
                    df_city.at[i,'quantity']=0
        dfe =(pd.pivot_table(data=df_city,index='vehicle_id',values=['quantity'],aggfunc={'quantity':'sum'}).reset_index())
        df_out.at[k,'country']=df_city.at[i,'countryss']
        df_out.at[k,'city']=c
        df_out.at[k,'all_waiting_for_parts']=dfe['vehicle_id'].nunique()
        df_out.at[k,'actually_waiting_for_parts']=dfe[dfe['quantity']>=1]['vehicle_id'].nunique()
        k=k+1

    return df{noformat}

*FYI from IBFD 21 October 2025* (note Italy has signed the [GIR-MCAA|https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-issues/tax-transparency-and-international-co-operation/gir-mcaa-signatories.pdf]):

Italy; European Union

_Report from Giulia Gallo, Principal Associate, IBFD_

Ministry of Economy and Finance Issues Decree on GloBE Information Return Filing

The Ministry of Economy and Finance has issued a decree outlining the procedure to be followed by qualifying taxpayers subject to the top-up tax (_imposizione integrativa_) to submit the GloBE Information Return (GIR), as provided by Legislative Decree No. 209/2023, which transposed into domestic law the Minimum Taxation Directive (2022/2523) (_see_ [+Reform of International Taxation Rules in Depth: Italy Enacts Minimum Taxation Directive (10 January 2024)+|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/tns_2024-01-10_it_4]).

Subject to certain exemptions (_see_ [+Italy Gazettes Ministerial Decree on Notification Procedure for GloBE Information Return Filing (10 March 2025)+|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/tns_2025-03-10_it_1]), each constituent entity located in Italy must submit the GIR to the tax authorities no later than 15 months after the end of the relevant fiscal year (or 18 months after the end of the transitional year, i.e. the first fiscal year of application of the GloBE rules; in this case the deadline cannot anyway expire before 30 June 2026).

The new rules are in line with article 8.1 of the [+Global Anti-Base Erosion Model Rules (Pillar Two)+|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/oecd_challenges_digitalisation_anti_base_erosion_pillar_2], taking also into account the clarifications provided by the [+Commentary to the Global Anti-Base Erosion Model Rules (Pillar Two)+|http://oecd_tax_challenges_pillar_two_commentary.pdf/], the [+Administrative Guidance on Article 8.1.4 and 8.1.5 of the Global Anti-Base Erosion Model Rules (January 2025)+|http://oecd_administrative_guidance_globe_rules_pillar_two_january_2025.pdf/] and the [+GloBE Information Return (January 2025)+|http://oecd_globe_information_return_report.pdf/]. Furthermore, the Ministerial Decree implements the provisions of the [+Amending Directive to the 2011 Directive on Administrative Cooperation (2025/872) (DAC9)+|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/tt_e2_41_eng_2011_tt__ad9] (_see_ [+DAC9 Published in Official Journal of the European Union (6 May 2025)+|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/tns_2025-05-06_e2_2]).

The Ministerial Decree of 16 October 2025, the explanatory report and the GIR model can be found [+here+|https://www.finanze.gov.it/it/archivi/notizie/dettaglio-notizie/Decreto-16-ottobre-2025-del-Vice-Ministro-delleconomia-e-delle-finanze/] (in Italian only). Further details will be reported upon publication of the Ministerial Decree in the Official Gazette.

h2. 🛴 The user disputes the city fine

Last updated: 15.10.25

*Issue tag:*

_Scooter/e-bike rider: I received a parking fine_

----

In this article, you can find the following information:

* [What are city fines?|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/627823714#what-are-city-fines]
* [How are city fines charged to riders?|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/627823714#how-are-city-fines-charged-to-riders]
* [Will the rider be blocked when they receive a fine?|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/627823714#will-the-rider-be-blocked-when-they-receive-a-fine]
* [Where can the rider check the city rules?|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/627823714#where-can-the-rider-check-the-city-rules]
* [How to handle disputes?|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/627823714#how-to-handle-disputes]
* [What if the rider insists we revoke the fine?|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/627823714#what-if-the-rider-insists-we-revoke-the-fine]
* [The user claims they weren't notified about the fine|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/627823714#the-user-claims-they-werent-notified-about-the-fine]
* [The user asks about the ride finish photo|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/the-user-asks-about-the-ride-finish-photo]

----

🌍 *Additional global information:*

All tickets regarding city fines should *not be redirected* to the city and must be solved by the CS agents. This also includes cases where the riders are complaining about general city regulations.

h3. What are city fines?

City fines will be charged when the city's rules are violated (e.g. when parking the vehicle). These are different from the fines that Bolt charges the riders when they finish the ride in a restricted area. 

City fines can be charged for the following reasons:

* Blocking pedestrians on a sidewalk
* Blocking intersections or road crossing
* Impeding public transport stops or entry/exit
* Not parked in a dedicated rack or parking area
* Parked in car parking areas
* Not wearing a helmet. Helmets are mandatory in:
** 🇭🇷 Croatia
** 🇨🇾 Cyprus
** 🇮🇹 Italy
** 🇷🇴 Romania (helmets are mandatory for users under the age of 16)

When communicating to riders who reach out to us about the fine, we need to make it clear that *these are issued* *by the city, not by Bolt.* 

*⚠️ Important:* For users in 🇸🇪 *Sweden*, avoid mentioning that the fine was issued by the city. Instead, inform them that the fine was issued because of non-compliant parking.

When Bolt receives a city fine, the fine details will be added to Admin, and based on the information, the potential rider who violated the rules will be automatically identified. The OPS team member then reviews the order and decides whether the fine is justified. 

*Important:* If the rider also received a [fine from Bolt (for finishing the ride in a restricted area)|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360008729834] and disputes both fines, address those two issues (fine from the city and fine from Bolt) separately in your response. 

----

h3. How are city fines charged to riders?

When the potential rider has been identified, they will be notified about the fine via email and in-app push notification. 

The fine will be charged automatically within 14 days from the day the rider received the email. If the rider wishes to dispute the fine (before or after being charged), they can contact our support.

*Important:* Riders will be charged from their original payment method. If they use ApplePay, the fine will be displayed as a negative Bolt Balance.

----

h3. Will the rider be blocked when they receive a fine?

The rider will be blocked *only from using Micromobility services* until the fine is settled. Other Bolt services can still be used. If the fine is cancelled or charged (after 14 days), the user will be unblocked automatically.

----

h3. Where can the rider check the city rules?

The link to the rules is linked to the notification about the fine. The rules can also be found under the Safety Toolkit in the app.

----

h3. How to handle disputes?

If the rider disputes a city fine, follow the steps below.

*Note:* This does not apply in case of fines charged by Bolt (for finishing the ride in a restricted area). In such cases, follow the [🛴 User reports getting a fine from Bolt process|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360008729834] instead. 

🌐 *Global:*

* Open the order in Admin panel. If you don’t know the order ID, search for it using the rider’s ID/phone number in _Admin panel > Rentals > Micromobility > Orders_
* Open the _Fines_ section (next to _Order logs_)
* Check the reason for the fine and the payment status, e.g. Completed, Pending. The list of reasons is available under the [What are city fines?|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/627823714#what-are-city-fines] section above
* Decide whether the fine is charged correctly or not
** For example, if the fine was charged due to the vehicle blocking pedestrians on the sidewalk, check the photo on the Admin panel order page and try to see if the vehicle was parked in the middle of the sidewalk, not on the side of it
** If you’re unsure where the vehicle was parked (e.g. the fine was charged for parking at a public transport stop), you can open the location on Google Maps and use the street view
** If you’re still unsure whether the fine is justified after the investigation, escalate the ticket to Tier 2 in Beehive. Leave your question in the ticket's internal notes. *Tier 2:* Review the ticket, if the justification is clear, leave notes for Tier 1; if not, follow the investigation guidelines, take over the case, make a decision, and continue with the process.
* If you decide that the fine should be revoked, Refund the user:
** If the payment status of the fine is _Completed_, refund the amount of the fine:
*** Go to _Admin panel > Rentals > Micromobility > Order > Fines_ scroll down to _Refunds_, select _Bolt Balance_ or _Original payment method_ (depending on the user's preference), leave a comment under _Refund Reason_ and click _initiate fine refund_.
** If the payment status is _Pending_:
*** Copy the Order or User ID, Go to _Admin panel_ > _Rentals_ > _Micromobility_ > _Users_ > _Fines_
*** Click _Open Filter_ and search for the fine using the User ID or order ID. Then click on Cancel Fine.
* If you decide that the fine was charged correctly, advise the rider accordingly and don't revoke the fine
* Leave a comment on the rider’s profile with the outcome and the ticket link

*🇳🇴 Norway:*

* If user disagrees with the fine they should contact the _City Environment Agency/Municipality_ to appeal the fine through the [website|https://www.oslo.kommune.no/gate-transport-og-parkering/parkering/klag-pa-bot/]. The fine includes the _Licence plate_ and _Case number_ needed to send the appeal. If the user has any questions or needs further assistance, they should contact the City Environment Agency/municipality.

🇸🇪 *Sweden:*

* Users who dispute fines must *never* be referred to the city. All fine-related disputes must be solved internally. Only Bolt can cancel the fine.

----

h3. What if the rider insists we revoke the fine?

Once you’ve ensured the fine cannot be revoked, clarify that it was charged due to violating the city rules and avoid going back and forth with the user.

If the rider mentions issues with the city rules (for example, they mention that the rules are unjustified), explain that Bolt can not change city rules and, as such, can not change them or the fine.

----

h3. The user claims they weren't notified about the fine

If the user claims they were charged but not notified about the fine, check if the email was sent:

* Go to [sent emails in Admin|https://admin.bolt.eu/email/Emails/sentEmails/]
* Enter the user's email in the search box

*If the email was sent*

* Ensure the user's email address in the app is correct
** email can be edited by opening the profile in the Bolt app
* The email didn't end up in the spam folder.

*If the email was not sent*

* On the order page in Admin, click on the _Fines_ tab
* Copy the number in the drop-down under "Select fine"
* Open the [Billing Document|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-document/invoices?tz=Europe%2FPrague&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22created_from%22%3A1741185212.414%2C%22created_to%22%3A1741271612.414%7D%7D] in Admin
* Paste the order number into "Order ID" and select the date of when the fine was issued ("Created from:" *one day before the fine was issued*, "Created to:" *one day after the fine was issued*, as the filter takes the exact time into account)
* Click on the PDF symbol on the right to download the fine invoice
* Send the fine invoice to the customer
* After sending the invoice, delete it from your computer. No further action is necessary.

----

h3. The user asks about the ride finish photo

If the user asks about the ride finish photo, inform the user that they should receive it together with the email about the fine.

If the user claims they haven’t received the ride finish photo:

* Go to the _Order_ page and check if there is the ride finish photo available
** *Ride finish photo available:* escalate the case to [Tech Support via their Service Desk|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/2/group/104].
** *Ride finish photo unavailable:* The user has been released from the obligation to take the final photo. If the user disagrees with the fine, refund the fine amount.

*Mentioned alternative Approach:*

# *Use* {{owned_by_driver_id}} *in the company table (the one from the description):*
By adding {{owned_by_driver_id}} to the *company*, we can remove the {{is_substitute}} flag from the *driver* table.
To identify substitute drivers, we simply check if their company has an {{owned_by_driver_id !== null}} — this indicates that all other drivers in that company are substitutes.
# *Keep* {{is_substitute}} *in both the company and driver tables:*
Alternatively, we can add an {{is_substitute}} flag to the {{company}} (instead of driver ID) while retaining it in the {{driver}} table.
In this setup, the driver without the flag within a company would be the owner, and all others would be substitutes.



*Note:*

Having both {{owned_by_driver_id}} and {{is_substitute}} fields introduces redundancy and increases the risk of data inconsistencies.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thanks for reaching out.

The quickest win is behavior-based controls. For fake orders we usually cap cancellations using new account details + the account’s own cancellation velocity. Penalties typically escalate from temporary blocks to hard-blocks. We can also factor device relations as a supporting signal, but it can be noisy and not reliable as a primary driver.

On verification, we don’t recommend triggering verifications off cancellations. Verified users can still generate fake requests. Verification fits better for user order requests, once we have a solid pattern.

I’d recommend starting off with stricter thresholds for the duration of the strike, after which we can leave a more lenient cancellation threshold as a baseline.

Here are the reasons that made me believe that this is correct (I could have shaped how we do simulations differently, had it been more transparent to me).

So there are two sources of error: bias and noise. It turns out that there are special terms for it. 

* *Bias* refers to epistemic uncertainty (error related to model misspecification, failing to reproduce the actual DAG)
* *Noise* refers to aleatoric uncertainty (error related to the fact that data is being too spread out/available in small quanitites => bad opportunity to do statistical inference)
** Note that multicollinearity also lives inside Variance (not bias)

Previously – I was trying to build a simulation tool that would holistically assess both (just because we were trying to build an integral tool).



But recently I came to understand that:

* Parameter variance in simulations is quite close to vmax intervals of the models themselves
** In some cases it is not very close. But we have to remember that when doing simulations I try to benchmark the noise and I might be not optimal in it 
* I got to know theory that bias and noise are separable. 

*How error (noise) reflects in coefficients (for frequentist, i.e. maximum likelihood).*  

!Screenshot 2025-10-22 at 16.05.00.png|width=278,alt="Screenshot 2025-10-22 at 16.05.00.png"!

*How error reflects in posterior (i.e. intervals)*

!Screenshot 2025-10-22 at 16.13.49.png|width=271,alt="Screenshot 2025-10-22 at 16.13.49.png"!

So we have a situation where it looks like we could be using noise from the models (vmax intervals) instead of simulations, and this could give us lots of convenience:

* Bayesian intervals – more interpretable
* Overall intervals  – more accurate (because those are based on real residuals of the model and not my approximate assessment of it)
* Process – simpler (big chunk of simulations preps was trying to quantify noise semi-manually, that could as well be a challenge for giving over the simulations to vertical team)



At the same time – we do not throw simulations away. They should help us understand:

* (operational) bias of the model due to tourists and other externallities (you cannot do it within a model itself)
* (methodological/research) which model specification is better (larger period/curve shape/etc)



[https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1oQ6olp-lLpQscZ2JthZ-wGGoX0czvzoo3YoCH1rqaoU/edit?usp=sharing|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1oQ6olp-lLpQscZ2JthZ-wGGoX0czvzoo3YoCH1rqaoU/edit?usp=sharing|smart-link] ==> Slides where I just made those pictures



*Note*: There might still be something I do not know (i.e. noise might still have some additional effect that I do not see), but there’s also always an argument that uncertainty is benchmarked not exactly precisely when we do simulations.

Hi [~accountid:637f26822acfad92d7b13ddb] ,

Thanks a lot for your input. I completely agree that standardisation across countries is essential, and my intention has always been to stay aligned with the group-wide approach while accommodating the practical nuances of local requirements.

To clarify the reasoning behind the proposed setup; in Switzerland, the daily allowance is meal-based sometimes emphasising the trip made within some specified time frame (travelling before 7:30 am or stay overnight to be able to claim breakfast, 12:00 to 13:30 for lunch etc) . Employees are entitled to claim specific meal allowances (Breakfast, Lunch, Dinner) depending on their travel circumstances. However, it’s not technically feasible for the FinTech team to enable a time-based configuration at the moment, which is why we’re proposing a simplified approach. Still, we cannot eliminate the meal-based logic, as it directly stems from local compliance requirements.

The approach I outlined aims to balance local regulatory needs, technical feasibility, and user-friendliness. Unlike in the UK, where the government allows prorated calculation based on travel hours (5 hours, 15 hours, overnight etc) , Swiss authorities require explicit recognition of meal-based entitlements. Attempting to negotiate a different arrangement would likely be disproportionate in terms of effort and resource allocation for the value it would bring.

That said, while the proposal may not meet 100% of the theoretical time-based criteria (e.g. only granting lunch allowance if travel covered the prime lunch hours 12:00–13:30), this is more close we could reach to be compliant. We can support this through a clear employee guidance document. We’ve successfully used a similar educational approach in the UK to ensure accurate and compliant claiming behaviour.

Regarding your second point, this is exactly what we’re proposing for overseas travel. To avoid excessive manual input (e.g. selecting 15 meal boxes for a 5-day trip), the system will pre-populate the full allowance based on departure and arrival times. Employees will then be able to declare if lunch or dinner was provided, and the respective deductions will be made automatically. For domestic travel, however, such automation isn’t practical, employees may only travel during part of the day (e.g. lunchtime), so it wouldn’t be appropriate to prefill or grant them the breakfast allowance. Doing so could raise compliance concerns with authorities and hypothetically might require in some cases that employees will have to enlist these as taxable benefit in their personal tax return.

Please feel free to discuss this further with me if anything remains unclear. Our next step is to confirm with the FinTech (WD) team whether the proposed configuration works technically, so that the Expense management team can proceed with testing before we move into the communication phase with the People Partner.


*Warm regards,*

Subarna

Hi [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e], thanks for your prompt response. Please see my comments to your question below. 

# *Request:* To better understand the risks, could you please confirm:

* How difficult would it be to update our process to not request or report the country of birth when a valid TIN is available? Would the absence of the country of birth in the report, where a TIN is provided, lead to report rejection?

As a general rule, under the DAC7 we should not collect country of birth if TIN / personal code is available. I understand this is also our approach, i.e. we do not collect place of birth if TIN / personal code is available - [~accountid:712020:fb07882f-e7b7-4ccc-a944-5b44db14f802] [~accountid:61b10873c75da8007263c3ec] please confirm. 

The difficulty is that the Estonian tax authorities do not allow the country of birth to be an empty field, i.e. the validation of the XML cannot pass when we submit the report in EMTA's website if the country of birth is empty for any individual. So it’s something that should rather be fixed on the EMTA side. I understand EMTA won’t be looking into this as they are satisfied that their “fix” of using a country of residence is, in any event, a reportable field. 

Separately, I have a follow up question relation to 2 & 3. We have reported Estonia as the country of birth for individuals who are not resident in Estonia as an error. If we now submit corrections to update this field to reflect the actual country of residence instead, would that be considered something to trigger a notification under GDPR, requiring us to inform the affected sellers that their personal data has been amended? Note that we have already reported the sellers’ tax residence under the relevant field, which is a required field under the DAC7 as I have noted above. 

I’m also conscious that, where we already have the seller’s TIN, there should be no requirement to report the place of birth in the first place. This means we may have sellers whose reported place of birth (i.e. place of residence) as a “fix” does not match their actual place of birth, which could lead to questions from sellers, given that the “corrected” data reported would in fact be incorrect.

Adding the query and results below. Tagging [~accountid:5ce7b2073f4d610fdf029c16] to ask for pointers on what I can improve in my approach. 

Note: I am checking only credit card companies, excluded postpaid.
{{ bibc.invoice_type = 'claim'AND bibc.credit_limit = 0}}

||Metric||Count||Interpretation||
|Total Spanish companies analyzed|*176*|All businesses signed up in Spain (signup_country = 'ES')|
|Companies with only foreign orders|*74 (~42%)*|Never placed an order in Spain|
|Suspected legit among those|*~30 (~40% of foreign-only)*|Known good, legitimate operations|

That is roughly *17% false-positive rate overall* if we flag all foreign-only companies as “fraud”. 
Or about *40% false positives* within the “foreign-only” subset itself. Meaning 4 in 10 flagged accounts are actually good.


{noformat}WITH window AS (
  SELECT DATE_ADD('month', -2, CURRENT_DATE) AS start_date
),
companies AS (
  SELECT
      bbc.id AS business_id,
      bbc.name AS business_name,
      UPPER(TRIM(bbc.country)) AS signup_country,
      bibc.balance AS balance_native
  FROM ng_public.business_business_company bbc
  JOIN ng_public.business_invoicing_business_company bibc ON bbc.id = bibc.id AND bbc.country = bibc.country
  WHERE bibc.invoice_type = 'claim'AND bibc.credit_limit = 0
),
orders AS (
  SELECT
      CAST(split_part(co.payment_method_id,'-',1) AS bigint)     AS business_id,
      UPPER(TRIM(co.country_code))                               AS order_country,
      co.created
  FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co
  JOIN window w ON co.created >= w.start_date
  WHERE co.payment_method_type = 'business' AND co.country_code IS NOT NULL
),
country_stats AS (
  SELECT
      o.business_id,
      COUNT(*)                                                            AS orders_total,
      SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_country = c.signup_country THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS domestic_orders,
      SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_country <> c.signup_country THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS foreign_orders,
      COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.order_country <> c.signup_country THEN o.order_country END)
        AS foreign_distinct_countries,
      array_distinct(
        array_remove(
          array_agg(CASE WHEN o.order_country <> c.signup_country THEN o.order_country END),
          NULL
        )
      )                                                                   AS foreign_country_list,
      MIN(o.created)                                                      AS first_order_at,
      MAX(o.created)                                                      AS last_order_at
  FROM orders o
  JOIN companies c ON c.business_id = o.business_id
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  c.business_id,
  c.business_name,
  c.signup_country,
  cs.orders_total,
  cs.domestic_orders,
  cs.foreign_orders,
  CAST(cs.foreign_orders AS DOUBLE) / NULLIF(cs.orders_total, 0) AS foreign_order_share,
  cs.foreign_distinct_countries,
  cs.foreign_country_list,
  cs.first_order_at,
  cs.last_order_at
FROM country_stats cs
JOIN companies c ON c.business_id = cs.business_id       
WHERE c.signup_country = 'ES'AND cs.foreign_orders > 0
ORDER BY cs.foreign_distinct_countries DESC,
         cs.foreign_orders DESC,
         foreign_order_share DESC,
         cs.last_order_at DESC
LIMIT 200{noformat}

Action steps:

h4. 1. *Decide How to Exchange Certificates*

* The police have shared their public certificates via [Global Trustpoint|https://www.globaltrustpoint.com/de].
* Bolt needs to provide its own S/MIME public certificate so the police can encrypt emails sent to Bolt.

h4. 2. *Obtain an S/MIME Certificate*

* You can purchase or obtain an S/MIME certificate from a trusted Certificate Authority
* The certificate is typically issued to a specific email address.
* IT or Security teams should manage this centrally.

h4. 3. *Set Up Encryption in Email Systems*

* The certificate must be installed in Bolt’s email system (Beehive)
* When enabled, emails to the police can be automatically encrypted and signed using S/MIME.

h4. 4. *Send Bolt’s Public Certificate*

* Once ready, Bolt should send its public S/MIME certificate (not the private key) to the German police.
