The first one is to detain or take other actions based on the right holder’s application. Once detecting export or import of goods is suspected of infringement, the right holder may report to the Customs, provide relevant guarantees, and request for detention of the goods. As this would require accurate clues and investigation beforehand, it is rare for the right holder to chase and detain the import/export of infringing goods. In practice, it’s more common for the Customs to take Ex Officio action on the infringing goods, which is the second method to enforce the IP right. When the Customs department discovers that imported/exported goods are suspected of infringement upon IP rights in the record, it will notify the right holder of the possible infringement. And the right holder should inform the Customs whether to detain the goods in three working days. If yes, it should also provide relevant guarantees. Hence, we think the risk of detention by the right holder’s report is not high, but there is a chance that the Customs will discover the exportation of Bolt Food bags and inform the right holder.2. We agreed that goods manufactured under the OEM mode do not constitute infringement upon registered trademark in China, because the goods either have a chance to enter the Chinese market and or be available to the Chinese customers. The trademark affixed on the goods is not identified by the public, let alone causing confusion as to the source of the products. This opinion and determination have occurred in precedents of court cases, we believe the court’s opinion in precedents would have a certain effect on the determination in similar cases in the_ [_future.In_|http://future.In] _case the goods are detained by the Customs, the client can request to release the goods with a margin and provide evidence proving the goods do not constitute infringement. The evidence could be the OEM manufacture agreement of the bags, trademark registration certificate of Bolt Food in the destination country/territory, and other materials that can prove all of the goods are solely to be exported. For example, the amount of manufactured products indicated in the agreement conforms to the amount of exportation. In practice, if there is solid evidence proving the non-infringement, the Customs will release the goods. In some complex cases, the Customs will tend to deny the infringement and inform the right holder to bring a lawsuit before the Court, and they will take necessary action based on the court’s order. In case the right holder doesn’t file a relevant request with the court within a prescribed period, the Custom will release the goods.3. Unfortunately, the trademark was registered on June 21, 2022, which is not available to a non-use cancellation yet as it’s registered for less than three years. Since the client hasn’t used the trademark in China on relevant goods in Class 21, we’re afraid that the chance of an invalidation request is not high. Hi Kristiin,

Has this been discussed with the Internal IT team?

I doubt this is in the SRE team’s scope.

This seems more related to IT.

*Regarding tooltip vs. snackbar*

I tend to agree that tooltip feels more contextual. The user’s attention is already on the car illustration when they’re checking whether the driver is moving or not. Also, snackbars can overlap or disappear, if another one appears or the countdown ends, so they’re less reliable.

So, my 2 cents: Tooltip is a more reliable and contextual design pattern for this communication.

I understand the idea to minimise effort to get feedback faster. But what’s stopping us from testing the tooltip? I believe it’s already an implemented component, so the effort should already be low. If the difference in effort between using a snackbar and a tooltip is truly significant (which I’d like to understand why), then perhaps we can make a tradeoff.

That tradeoff to me is a Snackbar that doesn’t disappear automatically and requires user acknowledgement like “OK”. But that tradeoff should only be to streamline the experiment. I would switch to a tooltip for the global rollout.



*Regarding the design and copy*

I’ve personally cancelled rides because the driver seemed not to be moving. Here’s my context of use: I order, step away for a couple of minutes (switch to other apps or just leave the phone), come back, and the car is still in the same place. At that moment, I cancel.

If I now see a message like _“Driver location will update soon”_ it doesn’t really reassure me. It raises more questions:

* Why is the location not updated? system issue or driver issue?
* How long should I wait before the update happens? And do you communicate to me when the location is updated?
* Wouldn’t it be faster for me to just cancel and rebook?

The current copy doesn’t really address these doubts or reduce uncertainty.

So, I’d suggest not rushing this. A bit more collaboration with design and UXW around communication design and copy is needed. Unless there’s an urgent reason to ship it fast, I’d recommend refining it first.

In short, if the user is entitled to a full or partial refund, *where to get it should be the users choice and not offered as a first option.*



+Detailed explanation:+

When a full, partial refund or compensation is given to a customer, we first ask where they want to receive it. There is a pop up banner that says Bolt Balance: immediately / Original payment method (2-5 working days/something like that). Is not that we don’t offer to refund users via Bolt Balance but they have the right to refuse, the correct way to put it is that we give them the option to choose.

So if the user chooses other repayment method, we proceed accordingly. Goodwill compensations are an exception, as they are not refunds but rather small compensations Bolt choses to issue users in order to minimise their frustration when the service has been provided without any issues.

The problem with Bolt Balance refunds is also that we cannot take it back afterwards. So, if the user is unsatisfied with the Bolt Balance refund  afterwards, Bolt has to choose either to refund again to the payment method (= double refund) or leave the customer unhappy (= risk of complaints/disputes). Another issue we had was that partial refunds were not possible with Bolt Balance, but perhaps not really relevant here and it might have been already fixed.

Hi [~accountid:5fa511639e35e50068b366f0] , it seems there’s some misunderstanding

I discussed this with billing so let me clarify what is and what is not possible.

A merger with a new VAT/NIF means a different legal entity. We must not change tax IDs on an existing profiles. A new Bolt Business account with the new billing details is always required.

Billing can’t “reissue” these past invoices to a new VAT number in PT. Those documents were issued to the old entity and must either stand as is or be credited.

The options:

# credit the invoices and forgive the debt.
# credit the invoices and transfer the balance to the new account
## This will not originate an invoice for the credited amounts, it’s just in the balance box, so the client probably will still not want to pay. But the balance will continuously show them owing us.
# credit the invoices and make a ticket to Finance for a one-off manual invoice that gets fiscalized by the accounting partner with the current details. 
## Given the amount at stake, I don’t think this will be accepted from Finance.

From a tax point of view, there should always be a credit of the unpaid invoices so that at least we do not have the VAT cost.

*My recommendation:*

Go with *Option 1*. Credit the rejected invoices and forgive the debt. Then invoice future periods only under a *new account* with the correct VAT details. 

In any case, the new account should be set up immediately if it’s not up yet. Until then, you’ll be building up unpaid balance because the invoice will use the old company details.



In all solutions, the past invoices are credited by billing, the difference is on the next steps - forgive debt, transfer balance, request finance for a manual fix.

Please reply here which option you want to go with.

+_Draft_+ 

*_“Bolt’s Approach to Supporting Vulnerable Customers_*

_Bolt recognises that some users - whether passengers, drivers, or delivery partners - may face circumstances that make them more vulnerable and may require additional support to access our services safely and fairly. While Bolt’s approach is not currently consolidated into a single, standalone ‘Vulnerable Customer Policy', we maintain a range of policies, training programmes and product features that collectively serve the same purpose - to identify, support and protect customers who may be vulnerable._

*_Identification of Vulnerability_*

* *_Mobility Impairments:_* _We proactively identify and serve passengers who require additional physical assistance. In the UK we have a Bolt Assist category to support passengers with mobility impairments or who would like a little more guidance when travelling independently. We developed a series of videos / guidance for drivers to complete in order to be able to join the category. The videos can be viewed here (_[https://bolt.eu/en-gb/driver/guide/accessibility-category-guidance/|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/driver/guide/accessibility-category-guidance/|smart-link] _) and were developed in collaboration with Disability Rights UK. Drivers must complete this guidance to then be able to offer trips on the Bolt Assist category which is designed specifically for older and disabled passengers. It includes information on the Equality Act, inclusive language, and how to offer additional assistance. This guidance was shared with Bolt’s Customer Support (“CS”) team when the category launched for further information on how to support disabled passengers if they were to make a complaint to Bolt._
* *_Customer Support Awareness:_* _Bolt is currently rolling out an 'Empathetic Communication: Train-the-Trainer’ programme, developed with Good Night Out, a UK-based NGO that supports organisations operating in the Night Time Economy_ a_nd the services that support their clients and staff. The training enables CS trainers to coach agents to recognise signs of distress, trauma, or vulnerability and to respond empathetically and consistently._ 
* *_Safety Incident Triage:_* _Our Safety & Support team has protocols for responding to reports of harassment, assault, or distress. These cases are handled by agents trained in trauma-aware communication._

*_Responding to Vulnerable Customers_*

* *_Accessible Service Options:_* _Bolt offers several tailored categories and programmes, including Bolt Assist for passengers with mobility needs (as mentioned above). Bolt also upholds offers such as Bolt for All, which offers discounted rides to low-income households._
* *_Empathetic Customer Service:_* _CS teams receive guidance and scripts for handling sensitive cases in a compassionate, flexible manner.”_

+Recommended Next Steps+

* If the above summary is still not sufficient for Airwallex, +we will need to prepare a formal policy/process that addresses vulnerable customers+. This will need to be based on the FCA guidance and Airwallex’s suggested approach which: 
** sets out a definition of vulnerability; 
** sets out a process map for CS agents to deal with a vulnerable customer (identify->flag-> adapt-> escalate); and 
** sets out how we monitor and govern our approach.

I did manage to find steps for this issue with VoIP calls.

*Prerequisites:*

* Rider and Driver have an active order (it can be in accepted state, no need to start a ride)

*Steps:*

* Rider kills the application process by swiping the Bolt Rides app out in recent apps
* Driver makes an outgoing VoIP call
* Rider receives a VoIP push notification that starts the application process
* When application is started the Rider makes an HTTP request to {{comms/voip/register}} endpoint that sends Sinch SDK registration status to our backend

*Expected result*

* The endpoint is executed successfully and the Rider app starts an incoming VoIP call

*Actual result*

* This endpoint returns {{{"code":503,"message":"NOT_AUTHORIZED"}}}
* The rider app triggers Auto Logout logic and terminates the user’s session



The issue is 100% reproducible with the JWT enabled. Without killing the Rider app process before receiving a call the bug is not reproducing. Quite likely when a VoIP push message triggered an application process to start it calls the {{comms/voip/register}} endpoint before the Auth Token is available, so it calls it with an empty {{Authorization}} header.

I’ll create a separate ticket in the Rider space to fix it.

*Court of Appeal Decision*

* Unfortunately, the Administrative Court of Appeal in Stockholm has *decided not to grant leave to appeal* in the case against the City of Stockholm.
* The decision is *not reasoned* (as is standard), so the court’s reasoning is unknown. This is a disappointing and, according to our external counsel, somewhat surprising outcome, given the limited case law on these issues.

*Possibility to Appeal*

* It is _possible_ to appeal this decision to the Supreme Administrative Court within three weeks, but that court _also_ requires leave to appeal and would not review the case on its merits.
* At best, it could decide that the Court of Appeal should have granted leave and refer the case back for a new review.
* The *chances of obtaining leave* to appeal are generally very limited - in this case estimated at *around 10–15%* - and the full process could take *9-12 months*.

*Next Steps and Recommendation*

* Following discussions with our external counsel, the *recommendation is not to appeal*, as a reversal is highly unlikely and the next permit period would be approaching by the time of any decision.
* External counsel can however explore other possible actions, such as informing the Swedish Competition Authority again. I’ll revert to [@roger.bjorkbacka|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U05QW62ETQQ] on that point.

* *Data Minimisation  Passenger Data Disclosure*: ✅

* *Data Sharing:* ⚠️ 
** We will be testing this category with Minicabit, who will be making reservations via the Bolt Business Platform.
*** i.e., Customer goes onto Minicabit website, and requests a trip. Minicabit concierge then books via the Ride Booker platform, using the ride details provided by the rider (the concierge will include name and flight number in the “Add a note to the Drivers” field).
** Presumably we will then be sharing driver data with the concierge, to enable the trip.
*** As such, we should be entering into a {color:#4c9aff}*Data Sharing Agreement*{color} (controller-to-controller, since the concierge has obvious agency)
* *Transparency*: ⚠️ 
** Business appears to be open to including the disclaimer language to cover the transparency gap.
** Although this is helpful, it now appears that the concierge will be making the order, not the passenger. As such, the passenger will not actually see this disclaimer, thereby rendering it slightly redundant.
*** I would recommend {color:#4c9aff}*amending the disclaimer language*{color} to the following: “_The passenger information that you provide here will be shared with the driver for the purpose of navigating their pick-up. By submitting this information, you confirm that you have notified the passenger that their details will be provided to Bolt. Bolt processes this information based on its legitimate interest in enabling transportation services. For further information, see our privacy notice available at_ [+_https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides_+|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides]”
*** This is not ideal from a privacy POV. However, the passenger is still covered by our privacy notice, so we just need to make sure they are aware that their details are being shared with Bolt (which would prompt them to check the privacy notice). Without visibility of an agreement, this disclaimer is the best halfway house to show we are at least trying to ensure that the passenger is informed (we took a similar approach with the Trusted Contact disclaimer).
*** NB. Contractual necessity may be difficult here since there is a degree of separation between Bolt and the passenger.
* *Live Location Tracking*: ✅ 
** Unsurprisingly, we will be tracking the driver’s location while they are ‘on foot’ in the airport, as this is still an active trip. The risk here is that some drivers may find this invasive / not expect this (even though there are good / obvious arguments for doing so).
** We can argue that this is covered in the driver privacy notice. We mention processing Geolocation Data, specifically “_We collect data about your precise and/or approximate geolocation… when you open and use the Bolt App_”. A common-sense reading of this would include while on foot during a ‘Meet & Greet’ trip. No need for a separate privacy disclaimer - this would be more of a ‘nice to have’ than a ‘must have’.
** Purpose here is to enable the transportation services, and legal basis would be either contractual necessity or legitimate interest. It is worth preparing a {color:#4c9aff}*LIA*{color} just in case, but this should not act as a blocker.
* *Retention*: (?) 
** Awaiting stakeholder confirmation re whether and how flight information will be retained in Admin.

Today I took the wiring prototype scooter completely apart, reinstalled every single cable one-by-one and tested the length and assembly of each. Taking also into account that we might want to ship “half assembled”. I checked against the drawings that had already been sent to Higo and even *confirmed for production without review.* 

I found a total of 5 cables that had to be adjusted:

* Dock extension cable - 130mm too short - technically would reach, but impossible to assemble due to assembly order. D2 cable fits perfectly, there was no point to even create a new BOM article. 
* Motor extension cable - 220mm too short - would not reach the motor. Impossible to use.
* Left turn signal - 100 too short. Possibly can be assembled, but high risk of damaging the brittle turn signal.
* Right turn signal - 100 too short. Same as above ☝️ 
* IOT + helmet lock splitter cable - 70mm too long (helmet lock connection). Not a big problem and can be used as is. Just need to tuck the extra wire into green tube.

In addition I found the following problems:

* Helmet lock connector was missing a blind plug
* Part numbers were messed up badly. There are different parts with the same part number. Randomly picking seemingly free numbers does not work, some of the picked numbers were already used in previous iterations of Dragon scooter. Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Hmm, but if it’s now under a partner company, then it shouldn’t necessarily matter, because the adjustment will be reflected on the provider company’s balance, but they can still see the compensation belonged to this location. 

Let’s say the provider had debt before and it was cleared before adding to provider company. In this case, the provider would be added to a provider company with 0 balance. 

But if a provider had debt and was added to provider company before clearing the debt, then the adjustment will be visible on provider company balance, but it will still technically compensate the same provider for that amount. As visible on the sales report, the compensation belongs to that provider, even if it appears also on the provider company balance.[^2025-08-25 -- 2025-09-01 Rukavichka Shpitalna Weekly Report.pdf]

Hi team, posting my thoughts from a privacy POV:

In principle, we are fine to proceed from a privacy POV, but just want to flag several third party marketing-related limitations in France that we’ll need to have in mind. This mostly impacts the operational setup, but want to make sure that it’s consistent with the deal structure.

1. *Legal Basis: Prior Opt-In Consent Required*

* Under the e-Privacy Directive and French law, you cannot rely on "soft opt-in" for third-party marketing to drivers. You must obtain opt-in consent from drivers before sending them third-party marketing communications (e.g., offers from external partners).
** This applies even if drivers are sole proprietors or business owners; they are treated as individuals for privacy purposes.

2. *Acceptable in-app marketing methods (consent vs. no consent)*

* In-app banners (shown to all users, not targeted individually) are considered general advertising, not direct marketing. Therefore, consent is not required for these banners.
** You may present third-party offers via non-targeted in-app banners or a dedicated "Partner Offers" section in the app.
* Targeted in-app messages, push notifications, emails, SMS, or app inbox messages that promote third-party offers do require prior opt-in consent.

3. *Consent management requirements*

* Drivers must be able to manage their marketing consents from a single place in the app (available in-app via settings).
* Drivers must be able to unsubscribe from marketing communications at any time, via an unsubscribe link in each message or through in-app settings.
* All marketing communications must respect the driver’s current consent status (i.e. if third party offers are disabled, we should not send direct marketing; however, generic marketing via banners is allowed).

4. *Summary Table: Consent by Channel for 3rd party marketing*

||Channel||Consent Required?||Notes||
|In-app banner (untargeted)|No|Considered general advertising|
|In-app banner (targeted)|Yes|Requires explicit opt-in|
|Push notification|Yes|Requires explicit opt-in|
|Email/SMS|Yes|Requires explicit opt-in|
|Partner Offers section|No|If not targeted, considered part of product feature|

See also:[https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PRODWIKI/pages/4090004297|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PRODWIKI/pages/4090004297|smart-link]

*In summary:*
For third-party marketing to drivers in-app in France, you must obtain opt-in consent for any direct marketing (targeted messages, push, email, SMS). General, non-targeted in-app banners or a dedicated offers section do not require consent. Drivers must always have the ability to manage and withdraw their consent easily.

h4. 1. *Overall assessment*

The request appears disproportionate and not fully justified under data protection principles.

While the lawyer cites a law which establish the right of advocates to obtain information needed to provide legal assistance, this does not automatically create a binding legal obligation on Bolt to disclose personal data. It provides a _right to request_ but not an _obligation to disclose_. Consequently, the cited law does not override GDPR/privacy principles nor establish a lawful basis under privacy law.

However, given the volume, sensitivity, and scope of the requested data, sharing would be highly intrusive and therefore disproportionate. It think that sharing extensive information on our internal processes could expose us, as a company, to risks too.

We need to reduce the scope of data we disclose + urge the lawyer to contact law enforcement and then we will cooperate.

h4. 2. *Proportionality and data minimisation*

* The request covers a wide range of highly sensitive data:
** Driver’s full identity, contact details, registration documents, and criminal record checks;
** Vehicle ownership and registration certificates (some of which may belong to third parties unrelated to the trip);
** Information on internal investigations and Bolt’s communications with law enforcement (which may contain confidential or privileged information).
* The lawyer’s purpose - preparation of a criminal defense case - does not justify such an extensive data disclosure by a private company like Bolt, especially without a court order or direct police request.

We can, at most, provide *some personal and non-sensitive information:*

* Confirm that trip took place on the specified date and route (we can provide driver full name but not provide other details);
* Explain that Bolt’s support and safety teams followed internal procedures;
* Add that any official reports or detailed data can only be released *to law enforcement directly*. *So, let’s reassure that we will cooperate with law enforcement.*

According to [Decreto-Lei n.º 156/2005|https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/legislacao-consolidada/decreto-lei/2005-34431675], Bolt has the following obligations in the case of a complaint in the physical books of the stores:

* 15 working days to send the original of the complaints form to the respective supervisory/regulatory body (ASAE). This can be done  by post or [email|https://www.asae.gov.pt/submeter-reclamacao.aspx], in this case digitised.
** With the original of the complaint sheet (red complaint sheet) we must also send any relevant documents or clarifications and the response that has been given to the consumer, where applicable.
** Keep the triplicate of the complaint as an integral part of the complaints book. If the consumer refuses to receive the duplicate complaint, Bolt must file the duplicate, mentioning this refusal.

The original complaint form may also be accompanied by explanations regarding the situation that is the subject of the complaint, including information on the follow-up that has been given to it.

Example query to fetch full table scans:


{noformat}-- Last 24h: queries whose actual plan included a full table or index scan
SELECT
  schema_name,
  digest_text,
  exec_count,
  ROUND(sum_latency/1e9, 2) AS total_latency_s,
  first_seen,
  last_seen,
  plan,          -- text EXPLAIN; look for TableFullScan / IndexFullScan
  plan_digest
FROM information_schema.cluster_statements_summary_history
WHERE last_seen >= NOW() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
  AND plan REGEXP 'TableFullScan|IndexFullScan'
  AND schema_name NOT IN ('INFORMATION_SCHEMA','METRICS_SCHEMA','PERFORMANCE_SCHEMA')
ORDER BY sum_latency DESC
LIMIT 200;
{noformat}

To my understanding this is a Partner (restaurant / merchant) we’re onboarding on Bolt Food platform. I can see in the Pdf doc you attached that Partner agreed to General T&Cs to Bolt Food Service with the Partner with no reservations. 

✅ The General T&Cs have a DSA (data sharing agreement) included when it comes to exchange of shared personal data (of Clients & Couriers) between us and Partner.



*The anticorruption agreement* 

States that Bolt & Partner inform each other of cases of breaches of the agreement

Section 2 – Personal Data Protection

* 2.1. When doing so, each party guarantees it already has proper data protection policies and systems (as separate personal data controllers) → doesn’t conflict with our roles under General T&Cs ✅ 
* 2.2. If Bolt holds personal data (e.g. employee or customer details), ORLEN cannot process that data without a separate, written agreement – and vice versa → personal data protection is covered in Schedule 2 of General T&Cs ✅ 
* 2.3. The only personal data that can be exchanged and processed between the two sides are business contact details (names, phone numbers, email addresses, etc.) that are necessary to carry out this agreement → correct ✅ 
* 2.4. As separate controllers, each Party must inform its employees or representatives whose data might be exchanged under this agreement → each party must have its employee Privacy Notice and is responsible for the processing of the personal data independently ✅ 



In summary, the Section 2 of the Anticorruption agreement is a data protection clause for 2 independent controllers processing minimal data, such as business contact details in limited circumstances. 

→ This aligns with Bolt data protection clauses in similar agreements.



There are no concerns from Privacy side – no need to propose amendments.

h2. *General summary:*

The Privacy and Product Legal teams have reviewed the draft position paper prepared in response to the European Commission’s public consultation on the *Digital Fairness Act* (DFA).

The document was initially reviewed by the Public Policy team, with Privacy pulled in subsequently to assess sections overlapping with data protection law, notably *Section 4 – Unfair personalisation practices*.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
The privacy team involved stakeholders from product-legal and set up a call with privacy, public policy, and product-legal to gather input for the consultation held on *29th of September*.
{panel}

*Topics raised by Product Legal during review:*

# Dark patterns
# Addictive design
# Specific features in digital products, such as in-app purchases (e.g. in video games)
# Harmful practices by social media influencers
# Unfair marketing related to pricing (dynamic and personalised pricing)
# Issues with digital contracts
# Simplification measures
# Horizontal issues

*Main concerns highlighted by Public Policy:*

* *Primary:* Dynamic pricing (Section 6) – risks of potential regulatory overreach and uncertainty around the boundary between legitimate price differentiation and unfair personalisation.
* *Secondary:* Unfair personalisation practices (Section 4) – concern over duplication and overlap with existing frameworks (GDPR, ePrivacy Directive, DSA, and UCPD).

h2. *Privacy review summary:*

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Privacy was looped in the consultation document after inputs by industry association were consolidated.* The Privacy team focused on the review of the positions relating to *Section 4 (Unfair personalisation practices)*, as the most relevant to data protection frameworks.

*Conclusion:* the Privacy team aligns with the current consultation positions and has *no additional comments* at this stage.
{panel}

h3. *Details:*

The review confirms alignment with the proposed position — namely that existing EU legislation (GDPR, ePrivacy Directive, DSA, and UCPD) already comprehensively regulates personalisation practices, including profiling, automated decision-making, and use of sensitive data.

*The current public consultation position highlights that:*

* Consumers already have mechanisms to control personalised advertising and pricing through consent and transparency obligations under existing law.
* Processing of sensitive data or personalisation targeting vulnerabilities (e.g. emotional or financial distress) is already restricted under *Articles 9 and 22 GDPR*, *Article 26 DSA*, and the *UCPD*.
* Introducing additional DFA obligations would risk overlap, regulatory fragmentation, and increased compliance complexity without tangible consumer benefit.
* The concept of “emotional stress” or similar subjective vulnerability categories should not be introduced as legal criteria, as they are not objectively definable or enforceable.

*Personalised / dynamic pricing clarification:*
The team supports the position that *personalised or dynamic pricing* practices are already addressed under existing consumer protection and data protection frameworks. Additional regulation under the DFA could create uncertainty around legitimate price differentiation.

Hello everyone,

Please find below a summary of the current status of the criminal proceedings, our position, and the next steps.

h4. +*Summary of the Incident*+

Bolt has been summoned as _civilly subsidiary liable_ in a criminal proceeding against the driver *Miguel Ángel Díaz Ramírez*, who is accused of committing a sexual assault offence against passenger *Laura González Fernández* during a trip booked through the Bolt app.

Being designated as _civilly subsidiary liable_ means that if the driver is convicted and fails to pay the compensation awarded to the victim, Bolt would be required to do so — in this case, *€3,000*.

The investigative phase (_fase de instrucción_) has concluded, and the Public Prosecutor has requested the opening of the oral hearing (_juicio oral_), which has been accepted by the Court.

At the time of the alleged incident, the driver was employed by one of our fleet partners, and it has been confirmed that the ride was booked via the Bolt platform.

h4. +Our Position+

We maintain that Bolt should *not* be held civilly subsidiary liable, as the company operates solely as an intermediary platform connecting passengers with service providers. Bolt has no contractual or employment relationship with the driver and therefore cannot be held responsible for actions occurring during the provision of the service.

While the compensation amount of €3,000 is relatively minor, our primary concern is the potential *precedent* this case could establish — namely, that platforms might be deemed civilly liable for the actions of individuals using their platform services.

h4. +*Next Steps*+

# *Review case law:* Examine recent Spanish court decisions applying *Article 120.4 of the Spanish Criminal Code*, which addresses the civil liability of legal entities for offences committed “in the course of their duties or services.”
# *Court liaison:* Contact the Court to confirm whether the _Auto de Apertura de Juicio Oral_ (order opening the oral hearing) must be collected in person or can be accessed electronically.
# *Entity clarification:* Verify which *Bolt entity* is designated in the proceedings as liable — specifically, whether this refers to *Bolt Operations OÜ* or another Bolt group entity.

Hey, our fraud rules worked differently on 2022, and it seems we didn’t count cancelled orders quite as we do now. The following is from a days worth of data.
Current daily AVG no_of_client_cancelled_orders of all cancel checks is roughly 0.81, with ~33% of users having done only 1 cancellation per 24h rolling period. Users doing 3 or more cancellations are ~0.07%.
Note: the cancellations we count are at the point of the check itself. Meaning that no_of_client_cancelled_orders = 1, means that the user has already cancelled a ride, and is trying to do so for a second time.



*Suggested thresholds for period of the Kumasi strike 24.10-27.10.* Matching the thresholds would result in a *full day block.*

* no_of_user_cancelled_orders > 4 or no_of_user_cancelled_long_orders > 4 or no_of_user_did_not_show_orders > 4 for all users.
* no_of_user_cancelled_orders > 3 or no_of_user_cancelled_long_orders > 3 or no_of_user_did_not_show_orders > 3 for users with less than 10 successful payments or users that are less than 7 days old.
Final cancellation would prompt a warning before the block. 

Under normal circumstances, only ~0.07% of riders reach to a 3rd cancellation and ~0.03% reach to a 4th cancellation within 24 hours. So these thresholds should be quite safe for good users.

Hey!
Correct - the approach has changed a bit. Until recently, there were 2 ways platforms like Bolt could defend narrow parity clauses (wide parity clauses have been illegal for a while):

# The “30% rule”: EU law  (VBER) says that if both Bolt and the restaurant each have less than 30% market share, we’re small enough that our agreements are _presumed harmless_ to competition  → So, below 30%, narrow parity clauses were usually fine.
# The “necessary for our business” argument (called “ancillary restraint”): Even if our market share was higher, we could say: “We need this clause to stop restaurants from undercutting us on their own website/at their store, so this clause is necessary for Bolt Food to function, therefore it’s not anti-competitive”

However, in 2024, CJEU found (C-264/23) that narrow price parity clauses are not really automatically “necessary for business”, therefore we cannot rely on the second argument anymore. So we removed this clause from all of our TCs, because as soon as we cross the 30% threshold, it’s risky.



As for these one-off agreements: my advice (if we want to use it for sure in this agreement), is to record why we think we don’t really have over 30% marketshare - e.g.  the “relevant” market is only the delivery of non-food items (we hopefully don’t have more than 30% there)

And same for Electronics as well

Also, the current wording is imo a bit too vague, especially the “The Partner agrees that the retail prices of its products listed on the Bolt Food Platform shall be identical to the prices offered in Euronics’ own online store *_and any other publicly accessible sales channels._* ” - imo, that makes it sound like we are limiting the prices on other sales channels (e.g. our competitors), which makes this a wide parity clause.

Adding the final profiling query here for phone numbers:



{noformat}-- Business phone number profiling, signups 

WITH signups AS (
  SELECT
    regexp_replace(get_json_object(d.input, '$.data.business_admin_phone'),'[^0-9]','') AS business_phone,
        d.meta.business_company_id AS business_company_id,
        d.created
  FROM archive_analytical.business_signup_check d
  WHERE d.created >= DATEADD(MONTH, -6, CURRENT_DATE)
  AND regexp_replace(get_json_object(d.input, '$.data.business_admin_phone'),'[^0-9]','') <> ''
),
fraud_deactivations AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT business_company_id
  FROM ng_public_spark.business_business_company_deactivation_log
  WHERE reason = 'fraud'
  AND created_date >= DATEADD(MONTH, -6, CURRENT_DATE)
),
phone_company_status AS (
  SELECT
     s.business_phone,
     s.business_company_id,
     CASE WHEN fd.business_company_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_fraud_deactivated
    FROM signups s
    LEFT JOIN fraud_deactivations fd ON s.business_company_id = fd.business_company_id
)
SELECT
    pcs.business_phone AS grp_key,                                  
    COUNT(DISTINCT pcs.business_company_id) AS count_of_companies,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN pcs.is_fraud_deactivated = 1 THEN pcs.business_company_id END) AS count_of_companies_with_fraud_deactivation,
    (COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN pcs.is_fraud_deactivated = 1 THEN pcs.business_company_id END) * 1.0)/ NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT pcs.business_company_id), 0) AS fraud_company_ratio
FROM phone_company_status pcs
GROUP BY 1
HAVING
    COUNT(DISTINCT pcs.business_company_id) > 5
    AND ((COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN pcs.is_fraud_deactivated = 1 THEN pcs.business_company_id END) * 1.0)/ NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT pcs.business_company_id), 0)) > 0.3
ORDER BY
    fraud_company_ratio DESC,
    count_of_companies_with_fraud_deactivation DESC{noformat}

Hey [~accountid:6218cbe4468c2e007170c08b] - a few notes on this ticket:



* Lets call it “Log Churn” instead of “Intend to Churn”. As it will be used by AM only when account gives us a feedback that is churning, then we just log this churn input, so it is already a confirmed intend.



* If the churn is permanent, AM selects the churn reason and sub-reasons accordingly, selects the locations it applies and saves. In this case, no opportunity is created.



* If the churn is temporary, AM selects the reasons and sub reasons, adds churn reminder, and saves. Churn opportunity comes back only on churn reminder date.



* If the account has a churn opportunity, and AM logs churn, then logged churn overrides the churn opportunities and close the opportunities for that account.
** If logged churn is for different child accounts vs the open churn opportunity, then it doesn’t affect the churn opportunity.
** If there is an overlap between logged churn for a child account, that is also part of the churn opportunity, then for that particular child account, churn reasons, sub reasons, status and churn reminder (if applicable) copied from the logged churn. For the rest, it stays blank until AM works on it.

Hi! To answer your question, I would start with a brief outline of how the system is built so that it is easier to explain why it appears to ignore car plate numbers.

When a driver takes a photo for car verification, the following happens:

1. *Verification* service (owned by verification team that you contacted before) checks that there is a vehicle on the image and reads the plate number. The key point is that this service *does not know* what is supposed to be the "correct" plate number — it simply reads it from the photo. In the [list of "verifications"|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity-trust/verifications/372fa0bc-b7fa-4610-a316-a9e2bf0766d1?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] it will always be listed as "verified" :white_check_mark: if there was any car with any plate number on the photo.
2. *Driver identity verification* service (that our team is responsible for) then takes the plate number that verification service found on the photo and compares them against the currently selected vehicle. If it does not match, it [marks the verification|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/8083470?tab=identifications] as failed. Importantly it does *not* suspend drivers in that case — this was explicit decision that the checks are too problematic to actually enforce.
Those services have *two different user interfaces in admin panel,* and the same verification can have two different statuses in those interfaces.

Let's look at the example of [this driver|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/8083470?tab=identifications], and car verification they did on 20 Oct 2025.

[In the verification service UI it is "verified"|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity-trust/verifications/372fa0bc-b7fa-4610-a316-a9e2bf0766d1?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] because there was a car on the photo (see the first two screenshots).

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Hi [~accountid:712020:1e9398f2-efcd-4dcd-8ece-28e6f8578e37] ,

Thanks for your message.

Since you already have green light from Central Legal to re-enable this feature in MT, the assessment we need to make is related to the impact in reclassification risks.

Referring to the Reclassification Risk Assessment prepared by Central Legal, *re-enabling the Driver Score*—even without any associated blocking—would r*educe our legal defensibility by approximately 10% i*n the context of potential reclassification claims in Malta.

However, the *confidence level attributed is “medium”*, which means that while it is clearly helpful, the precise extent of that benefit is unknown — as it has not yet been tested in Maltese courts. Realistically, we estimate the legal value of the feature sits *somewhere between 0% and 20%*, depending on how courts would interpret its impact on platform control.

That said, we are comfortable concluding that *this is ultimately a business decision. From a legal standpoint,* enabling the Driver Score in a non-punitive manner (i.e., without any operational consequences for drivers) i*s acceptable.*

However, w*hile a 10% impact might seem limited on its own, we would strongly advise the Team to take into account the cumulative effect of all recently enabled features*. As discussed in our meeting this week, the acceptance rate is already visible again, and there are ongoing considerations around limiting access to categories based on AR. While each of these changes in isolation may not present excessive legal risk, taken together they could significantly erode our overall defensibility in the event of reclassification claims.


In case you decide to move forward, here is the communication revised:

*_Subject:_* _Driver Score Now Visible in Your App_

_Dear Driver,_

_We’d like to let you know that the Driver Score (DS) feature is now visible again in your Driver App._

_This score is shown_ *_for your reference only_*_. It does_ *_not_* _affect your access to the platform, trip allocation, earnings, or account status in any way._

_Thank you for driving with Bolt._

_Best regards,_



Please do let us know what was decided by the business and, in case it is decided to move forward, let us know since when the feature is going to be re-enabled.

Thank you!

*Thinking out loud:*

* We might not need to target whether we are paying off or not.
* But we might want to target some specific curve accuracy, which can be achieved by:
** specify the required confidence/credible intervals
** run experiments that would guarantee us those intervals (see plot)
** pass experiment result toghether with uncertainty to the model
*** This will spit out the curve. And this will give a range of vmax-es. And from Martech3-1166 we know that as spend decreases, uncertainty also decreases (so we can our curve shape assumption works as an assumption for uncertainty across all levels of spend)
* If we do it this way, we should expect our confidence in the curve to be “high“ no matter what is the actual observed effect (based on experiment results)
* This will make decision-making entirely Bayesian. But would come with some specific questions:
** Where do we discern something from randomness?
*** Would  the curve vmax = 3 still be eligible to some spend?
** How does this work with Causal Impact results?
*** Should be seamless (posteriors go to priors)
*** But how does prior_level_sd selection work here? And how does the approach where we fit prior_level_sd to False Positive Rate relate? How do we define a proper prior_level_sd without False Positive Rate (or is matching the distributions enough)?
*** General question:
**** Previously we were using False Positive rate, because Causal Impact would return some small effect with probability just slighter than 0.5 (e.g. 0.65), which (with assumption that (1)ads not generate negative effect (2) the distribution of effect is symmetric) would lead to decision to start spending. Especially if this small effect can practically be useful. 
**** But probably the answer is: our posterior for Causal Impact was wrong. It should reflect that negative effect is possible as zeros, so that those zeros also participate in weighted mean for decision to spend.

Hi [~accountid:5acb1f48d8b95a2b34f150a8] ,

To summarise, we’ve received a small claim from a rider concerning a trip from Stansted Airport → London on 11 October 2025. The rider alleges that the driver’s vehicle broke down several times and ultimately abandoned her on a highway, instructing her to “order another taxi.” She seeks *£305.78*, broken down as follows:

|*Claim Item*|*Amount*|
|Refund for incomplete / unsafe journey|£56.09|
|Cost of alternative taxi|£14.69|
|Compensation for distress / inconvenience|£200.00|
|Court claim fee|£35.00|
|*Total*|*£305.78*|

# +*Key Facts Identified*+

* The trip *did not reach its intended destination*. The drop-off was at 492B Watford Way NW7 2PX rather than the intended 59 Mill Lane NW6 1NB — approximately *5 miles apart*.
* The driver uploaded a new vehicle to their Bolt account two days later (13 October 2025). The trip in question was the final journey completed using their previous car, suggesting the *previous vehicle may indeed have been defective*.
* Customer Support refused a full refund on the basis that the trip was “nearly complete”, though this may be difficult to defend given the substantial remaining distance and the rider’s abandonment on a highway.
* The rider was offered £2, later £5, and these were both refused.



# +*Options for Next Steps*+

*Option* :1_one_circle_red:  *– Defend the Claim in Full*

* We could argue that the issue arose from an unforeseeable mechanical failure and Bolt has limited liability under the T&Cs.
* {color:#36b37e}_Pros:_{color} Protects Bolt’s legal principle and deters inflated claims.
* {color:#ff5630}_Cons:_{color} Will require legal resources; potential cost may exceed the claim value; risk of court finding against us.

*Option* :2_two_circle_orange:  *– Partial Settlement (Without Admission) ← Recommended* :green-check: 

Offer a *commercial settlement of £75 – £100*, at least covering the incomplete-trip refund and alternative taxi, *without admission of liability*.

* {color:#36b37e}_Pros:_{color} Cost-effective by avoiding further legal costs, proportionate to likely court outcome, preserves goodwill.
* {color:#ff5630}_Cons:_{color} Could encourage expectations for similar settlements.

*Option* :3_three_circle_green:  *– Settle in Full*

Pay £305.78 in full without admission, citing safety and customer-experience considerations.

* {color:#36b37e}_Pros:_{color} Eliminates litigation risk.
* {color:#ff5630}_Cons:_{color} Inconsistent with prior approach and may incentivise inflated claims.



# +*Recommendation*+

Given the low claim value relative to potential legal costs of a full defence, we recommend *proceeding with Option 2 – a partial settlement (£75–£100)* on a *without-admission basis*.

This approach balances cost-efficiency (avoiding disproportionate legal spend) and demonstrates reasonable customer-care.

However, *the decision is ultimately up to you/the business so please do let me know your thoughts.*

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Thanks all - my thoughts are as follows:

* *In-person meetings*: No caught by electronic direct marketing legislation. No need for prior consent from fleet owners ✅ 
* *Phone call*: May fall foul of telemarketing laws, so opt-in consent to marketing here may still be needed ⚠️  As such, we would have to take one of the following two approaches:
** +Option (a)+ Check if the fleet owner has previously consented to third-party marketing (i.e., partner offers), including via the phone. If they have, we can provide the ad company’s contact information over the phone.
** +Option (b)+ Alternatively, we could inform the fleet owner about the ad company during a general service call (i.e., a call not specifically to inform them about this ‘earnings opportunity’), +_provided that_+ we take the following steps to obtain their consent first:
*** (i) During the call, explicitly ask the fleet owner _“Would you like an intro to our partner offering in-car tablets? If yes, may I share their contact information with you?”_.  If they say yes, _then_ share the name of the ad company and their contact information verbally. If they say no, do not do so.
*** (ii) If the fleet owner consents over the phone per the above, keep an auditable record of the fact that they have provided this consent.

I would flag that Option (b) above is not perfect from a compliance POV, but it would mitigate most of the risk here. Ultimately, the easiest solution from a compliance POV would be to stick to in-person comms.

Hi [~accountid:620e4df5a713ab0068139e4a], I have taken a look and DA have rejected some of my amends. There are 4 points to consider and I have copied these below for completeness, alongside my proposed next steps:



# *Scope and purpose*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: Bolt’s NDA references a general “Relationship” or discussions about a possible relationship whereas DA’s is specific to “working together to obtain further detail of Bolt’s operations at Dublin Airport.” DA’s version is narrow — protection only applies to info shared _for this defined purpose_, leaving room for argument that other disclosures (e.g., operational data shared later) are outside scope.
* {color:#36b37e}Previous resolution (rejected){color}: I have broadened the scope to include all information shared “in connection with discussions or commercial relationships between the parties.”
* Next steps: ➡️ DA have added a defined term of “Purpose”. This doesn’t resolve my original concern, however I don’t see this as a blocker. *Please could you confirm if the business is comfortable taking the risk that disclosures outside of conversations specifically regarding Bolt’s operations at Dublin Airport will not be protected by the confidentiality agreement?*



# *Definition of Confidential Information*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: DA’s agreement requires that oral disclosures must later be confirmed in writing and marked “CONFIDENTIAL.” DA’s definition narrows protection — unconfirmed oral or unmarked information may not be protected.
* {color:#36b37e}Previous resolution (rejected){color}: I have removed that requirement.
* Next steps: ➡️ This means that Bolt will have to be +*extra careful*+ and make sure that +*all*+ disclosures that we want to be kept confidential are in writing and marked as confidential. Again, I do not see this as a blocker, but it is something to definitely be aware of - *please can you confirm if the business is comfortable accepting this obligation?*



# *Liability cap*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: Bolt’s NDA includes no liability cap, whereas DA’s agreement caps liability at €50,000 total for any breach (Clause 9). This significantly limits DA’s exposure if it breaches confidentiality, but limits Bolt’s ability to recover damages. This is highly disadvantageous for Bolt.
* {color:#36b37e}Previous resolution (rejected){color}: I have removed this cap in the first instance. However, if DA reject this amendment, we can look to increase the cap.
* Next steps: ➡️ I have increased the liability cap from €50,000 to €100,000. 



# *Assignment and affiliates*

* {color:#ff5630}Concern{color}: DA’s agreement prohibits assignment without written consent. This restricts flexibility for Bolt’s corporate structure.
* {color:#36b37e}Previous resolution (rejected){color}: I have removed the need for consent (as in Bolt’s NDA).
* Next steps: ➡️ Again, I do not think this is a blocker. *Please confirm if the business is comfortable with the need to obtain consent* +*_if_*+ *the agreement needed to be assigned* (it may not even need to be assigned!).

{code:sql}WITH driver_compensations AS (
SELECT  
DATE(created) AS comp_date,
to_agent_id AS driver_id,
ROUND(SUM(sum_with_vat),2) AS compensation_amount_gbp
FROM ng_public.billing_ride_hailing_record 
WHERE created_date >= date '2025-08-04'
AND to_agent_type = 'driver'
AND "type" = 'national_living_wage_topup'
AND sum_with_vat > 0
GROUP BY 1,2
), 
orders AS (
SELECT 
co.created,
co.city_id,
co.id AS order_id,
CASE WHEN ot.state = 'finished' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS finished_order,
ot.driver_id,
dc.compensation_amount_gbp,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY date(date_trunc('week',co.created)),ot.driver_id ORDER BY co.created DESC) AS rn
FROM ng_public.company_order co
JOIN ng_public.etl_fact_company_order_try_state_log_transposed ot ON co.id = ot.order_id AND co.city_id = ot.city_id 
JOIN driver_compensations dc ON dc.driver_id = ot.driver_id AND date(date_trunc('week',co.created)) = CAST(DATE_ADD('week', -1, dc.comp_date) AS date)
WHERE co.created_date >= date '2025-07-28'
AND ot.created_date >= date '2025-07-28'
AND co.country = 'gb'
AND ot.driver_accepted IS NOT NULL 
AND ot.state IN ('finished','client_cancelled','client_did_not_show')
)
SELECT 
date(date_trunc('week',o.created)) AS order_week,
o.city_id,
APPROX_DISTINCT(o.driver_id,0.0041) AS count_drivers,
APPROX_DISTINCT(o.order_id,0.0041) AS count_orders,
SUM(o.finished_order) AS count_finished_orders,
SUM(o.finished_order)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(o.order_id,0.0041) AS finished_ratio,
ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN o.rn = 1 THEN o.compensation_amount_gbp ELSE 0 END),2) AS sum_compensation_amount_gbp
FROM orders o
GROUP BY 1,2
ORDER BY 2,1 DESC{code}

Hey, [~accountid:5e4cfe3b393ea90c94b40eb0] - right. Thanks for the comments below - I will address every single point that you raised.

# *NDA Executed*

The fact that the DSA is placed in a separate document does not necessarily mean it constitutes a separate undertaking. In cases like this, the DSA is not an independent agreement but rather an attachment to the main Agreement. Therefore, we typically include several clauses in the NDA that explicitly refer to the DSA as the part of the Agreement governing data sharing. For the future reference, please do not sign any Agreement/ NDA before the Privacy part has been already reviewed. 

Regarding this case, since you mentioned, that the Main Agreement is not yet in place and we are only exploring the option, are we planning to receive personal data at this stage? Or only after the Main Agreement has been drafted? If the latter, the Privacy input will be necessary only at later stages.

# *DSA*

As a starting point, please note that a DSA is concluded only in specific scenarios - not automatically whenever data is exchanged. The DSA, as a sub-agreement, imposes a number of obligations, to a great extent on the data importer, requiring them to comply with the provisions set out in it.

Secondly, with regard to the statement:

{quote}“Our drivers reaching out to Bastion Health Insurance through our platform is us sharing data with them.”{quote}

Please note that this is *not* accurate. We are not directly sharing any personal data with Bastion. Instead, we are merely facilitating a process through which drivers may independently share their personal data directly with Bastion Health Insurance. By enabling such contact, Bolt is not itself engaging in data sharing.

Given the above, having a DSA in place would not be beneficial - in fact, it would create unnecessary obligations for us, as it is Bastion Health Insurance who would, in this context, act as the data recipient (or importer) rather than Bolt. That is why, instead of concluding a DSA, we would rather insert several clauses into the Main Agreement. 

Looking forward to your reply!

However, certain local restrictions may apply, depending on the region and the current martial law conditions.

The sale and delivery of alcohol to military personnel are governed by general alcohol regulations and any additional limitations introduced under martial law. +The law does not require couriers or businesses to determine whether a recipient is a member of the Armed Forces. Moreover, sellers and couriers are not legally permitted to request confirmation of a person’s military status.+ This applies equally to in-store purchases and delivery transactions.

I will check further this case and any potential liability for Bolt/courier, but for now in these cases we could rely on the below mentioned clause from the T&Cs for the clients:

*_3.5.  The Client must comply with applicable laws, including the requirements applicable upon purchase of alcohol, tobacco, energy drinks or any other products requiring age verification._* _In case the Client wants to order products requiring age verification, he/she must confirm and/or prove his/her age as part of the ordering process. Further, the Courier delivering the Order and/or the Partner in case of self pick-up by the Client may refuse to hand over the products requiring age verification, if the Client does not present a valid photo identification proving that he/she is old enough to legally purchase the products._

At a later stage when we carry out the updates to the delivery T&Cs in Ukraine, I will also specifically include this point stating that Bolt and courier have no liability in such cases, and only client needs to make sure they comply with any applicable requirements.

25W43: Eater surge multiplier on Minimum Order Value

* *Done* - Define a new Dynamic Multiplier Type and corresponding settings for Small Order Fee:
** *Scope and value*: Adds SMALL_ORDER_FEE dynamic multiplier so small order fees can adapt to city busy ratios; aligns pricing levers across courier earnings, delivery fee, and small order fee.
** *Implementation and integration*: Extends DynamicMultiplierType, DynamicMultiplierGenerator, and DynamicMultiplierCron; repository, cache, monitoring, and event publishing updated; 
** *Configuration and defaults*: New SmallOrderFeeDynamicMultiplierSettings; feature off by default; conservative ranges set to 1 to 1 for multiplier and busy ratio to avoid behavior change.
** *Strategy support*: Works with CURRENT_BUSY_RATIO and AVERAGE_BUSY_RATIO, matching existing multiplier strategy patterns.
** *Quality and coverage*: new spec tests and component tests covering DB, cache, API; mirrors patterns used for other multiplier types. *All tests were created using Cursor as the AI Agent.*
** *Risk, rollout, and performance*: Backward compatible and gated by config; minimal performance impact by reusing existing infrastructure; consistent architecture for predictable maintenance.
* *Done* - Extend _delivery_fee_surging_ event config with a new property, describing where the config will be applied:
** *Scope and value*: Extending delivery_fee_surging targeting event to include all eater fee types, renaming it to EATER_FEE_SURGING and enabling surging for small order fees to improve pricing flexibility.
** *Implementation and integration*: Adds {{targeted_fee_name}} to select the fee the surge applies to. 
** *Configuration and compatibility*: {{targeted_fee_name}} defaults to delivery_fee for backward compatibility. Targeting can override city config for enablement. 
* *Done* - Remove "Excluded provider traits" feature:
** *Context*: Remove unused {{excluded_provider_traits}} from surge config.
** *Backend changes*: remote config was regenerated an all code that was using this field was removed;
** *Admin Panel changes*: simplified Admin Panel surge configuration by removing unused provider trait filtering.
* *In Testing* - Consume the updated targeting config and the new dynamic multiplier for small order fee:
** *Implementation and integration*: Extends loaders, builders, computation logic, repository and cache flows. Refactors shared config loading into {{loadSurgeConfig}} for reuse.
** *Configuration and compatibility*: Caching TTL is shorter when surge is active. Surged values are persisted.
** *Key behaviors verified*: Correct surge application only when enabled. Works for regular, dynamic, and laddered SOF including threshold transformation and MOV calculations. Distance based scenarios and multiple multipliers validated.
** *Quality and coverage*: new focused specs for SOF model and helpers. Integration tests cover surge, caching with DB verification, targeting overrides, and fee routing via {{targeted_fee_name}}. *All tests were created using Cursor as the AI Agent.*
** *Outcome*: A unified surging framework across eater fees with a safe default, clear routing via {{targeted_fee_name}}, and strong automated coverage for confident rollout.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

* First active date was just set (provider_first_active_date__c became non-null).

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Marten

*Solution summary:*
A unified, platform-specific accessibility approach for the Snackbar component - addressing screen reader support, keyboard and gesture interaction, semantic roles and best UX behavior.
{panel}



*Component Definition:*
Snackbar is a temporary, non-modal alert with:

* Title
* Description
* Up to 2 action buttons
* Auto-dismissal and optional manual dismissal

----

*Universal accessibility requirements*

||*Feature*||*Requirement*||
|Screen reader|Must be automatically read aloud when it appears|
|Focus|Should not receive focus by default unless required for urgent info or interaction|
|Dismissal|Supports auto-dismiss (minimum 5s, but subjectively I would recommend 8-10s), manual dismiss (button or gesture), and respects reduced motion settings|
|Actions|Max 2 clear, descriptive buttons (“Retry”, “Undo”) that are accessible by keyboard (Web) and accessible by gesture/focus (Mobile)|
|Reading order|Title → Description → Action buttons (if any)|

----

*Web React*

* *Role and semantics*:
** Use {{role="alert"}} + {{aria-live="assertive"}} + {{aria-atomic="true"}} on wrapper
** Do not auto-focus; content will be read by screen readers if live region is correct
* *Keyboard*:
** Allow {{Tab}} to reach action buttons
** Support {{Escape}} to dismiss

||*Requirement*||*Implementation*||
|Screen reader|Use {{role="alert"}} and {{aria-live="assertive"}} to ensure automatic announcement|
|Atomic updates|{{aria-atomic="true"}} ensures screen readers announce the whole update|
|Keyboard|{{Tab}} navigates to buttons
{{Escape}} dismisses|
|Focus|Do not auto-focus; let screen reader pick it up from the live region|
|Visual focus|Ensure buttons show clear focus outlines|
|Reduced motion|Animate in/out only if {{prefers-reduced-motion}} is false|

----

 *iOS native*

* *VoiceOver Announcement*:
** Requires manual announcement via {{AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility()}}
* *Traits*:
** {{accessibilityRole="alert"}} and {{accessibilityLiveRegion="assertive"}}
* *Action Buttons*:
** Must be {{accessible={true}}} and include {{accessibilityLabel}}

||*Requirement*||*Implementation*||

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

## The Parties agree that the following provisions of the DSA shall expressly survive termination of the Partnership Agreement and continue in full force and effect until the Egyptian Partner has permanently deleted all Personal Data in accordance with Clause 10.2.2:
### Clauses 1–3 (Purpose and Roles of the Parties);
### Clauses 9–15 (Data Importer Obligations, Security and International Transfers);
### Clauses 18–20 (Cooperation, Indemnity and Post-Termination Data Handover); and
### Annex 2 (Technical and Organisational Measures) and Annex 3 (EU Standard Contractual Clauses Framework); and
## Until deletion or anonymisation has been completed in accordance with Clause 10.2(b):
### the Egyptian Partner shall continue to handle any remaining Personal Data strictly in accordance with the DSA and Applicable Data Protection Laws;
### the Egyptian Partner shall cooperate fully with Bolt in responding to any Data Subject requests, authority inquiries or regulatory proceedings relating to the former operations of the Bolt Platform; and
### the Egyptian Partner shall notify Bolt without undue delay and in any event within forty-eight (48) hours of becoming aware of any suspected or actual Personal Data Breach affecting such Personal Data, in accordance with Clause 9(c) of the DSA.
## The Egyptian Partner shall not use, disclose or retain any Personal Data obtained under the Partnership Agreement or the DSA for any purpose other than as strictly required by Applicable Data Protection Laws. In particular:
### The Egyptian Partner warrants that it shall not, and shall procure that its personnel, Related Parties and service providers shall not, access, use or otherwise process any Personal Data relating to the Bolt Platform following completion of the deletion obligations. Any breach of this obligation shall constitute a material breach entitling Bolt to seek immediate injunctive relief in addition to any other remedies.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

h2. Colorado

The primary legislation is the *Colorado Privacy Act (CPA)*. The CPA establishes consumer privacy rights, controller and processor duties, and enforcement mechanisms to protect personal data of Colorado residents acting in an individual or household context. 

It applies to controllers that conduct business in Colorado or target Colorado residents and meet specific thresholds (processing data of *≥100,000 consumers* or deriving revenue from selling data of *≥25,000 consumers*). 

The Act does not create a private right of action; enforcement is vested in *the Attorney General and District Attorneys*. 

h3. Regulatory requirements:

||*Data Transfers to EU*||:green_circle:||EU Adequacy Decision, EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (*DPF*)
CPA does not contain any explicit provision regulating or restricting cross-border or interstate data transfers||
|*Data Localisation*|:green_circle:|No data localisation requirement.|
|*Legitimate Interest*|:green_circle:|The CPA does *not establish a closed list of legal bases* (such as consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, or legitimate interests). Instead, it imposes a *duty-based model*, meaning controllers must ensure that:
* Personal data are collected for *specified purposes* and limited to what is *necessary and relevant* to those purposes.
* Processing for new or secondary purposes requires *additional consent* from the consumer.
* Processing of *sensitive data* always requires prior *explicit consent*
_§§6-1-1305 to 6-1-1309_|
|*DSAR*|:green_circle:|Response time: without undue delay, and *within 45 days of receipt*. May extend once by another 45 days if necessary.
First request is *free of charge*; subsequent requests within 12 months may incur a reasonable fee.
The controller must issue a written explanation of its decision and inform the consumer of their right to contact the Attorney General if dissatisfied
_§ 6-1-1306(1)_ - lists all data subject rights
_§ 6-1-1306(2)_ - details how controllers must respond|
|*Registration requirements*|:green_circle:|No mandatory registration requirements.|
|*Group DPO*|:green_circle:|The CPA does not require designation of a Data Protection Officer.|
|*Data Sharing with Authorities*|:green_circle:|Controllers and processors may disclose personal data to comply with a civil, criminal, or regulatory inquiry, investigation, subpoena, or summons by federal, state, or local authorities.
_Section 6-1-1304(3)_|
|*Data Breach Notification*|:green_circle:|A notification must be made to the AG if the breach affects *500 or more* Colorado residents. _§6-1-716(2)(f)(I) of the Colo. Rev. Stat._
A notification is not required if an investigation determines that the misuse of information about a Colorado resident *has not occurred* and *is not likely to* occur. _§6-1-716(2)(f)(I) of the Colo. Rev. Stat._
The AG shall be notified in the *most expedient time possible* and without unreasonable delay, but *no later than 30 days* after the date of determination that a security breach occurred. _§6-1-716(2)(f)(I) of the Colo. Rev. Stat._
Reporting entities must direct their notice to the AG through the Breach Form.|
|*Privacy Notice*|:green_circle:|According to *_§6-1-1308(1)(a)_*, the privacy notice must include:
# *Categories of personal data collected or processed* by the controller or processor.
# *Purposes* for which each category of personal data is processed.
# *Instructions for exercising consumer rights* under _§6-1-1306_ - including:
#* How consumers can access, delete, correct, or opt out of data processing,
#* Controller contact information, and
#* How to *appeal* a controller’s decision.
# *Categories of personal data shared with third parties*, if any.
# *Categories of third parties* with whom personal data are shared|
|*Online Marketing*|:green_circle:|The CPA regulates *targeted advertising* and *the sale of personal data*. Controllers must: 
* Allow consumers to opt out of processing for targeted advertising or sale of personal data. 
* Clearly disclose such processing and provide an easy opt-out mechanism in their privacy notice.
* Respect a universal opt-out mechanism that allows consumers to opt out across controllers|
|*Biometric Data*|🔴|_6-1-1303(24)(b)_ - definition of biometric data
_6-1-1308(7)_ - consent to process biometric data
_§ 6-1-1303(5)_ - requires consent to be a clear, affirmative act - not passive acceptance or through dark patterns
*HB 1130 Privacy of Biometric Identifiers & Data Act* amends CPA. It requires a written policy:
* A retention schedule for biometric data and identifiers.
* A protocol for responding to a data security incident that may compromise the security of biometric data or identifiers, which includes a process for notifying consumers of the breach.
* Guidelines requiring the deletion of a biometric identifier (but not biometric data) on or before the earliest of: (a) the date upon which the initial purpose for collecting the biometric identifier has been satisfied; (b) 24 months after the consumer’s last interaction with the controller; or (c) no more than 45 days after a controller determines that the storage of the biometric identifier is no longer necessary, adequate, or relevant which is to be reviewed on an annual basis.
* The written policy must be *publicly available.*|

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten
