[~accountid:5e5cecb04befbd0c96cab72a] [~accountid:616ff0d5e79ff6006f3423de] Hey all, the core issue here is the invoice itself. If we look at IN-EE005-25-045033 for example, there are two lines with amounts -5.3466 and -0.386. When Telema is reading this invoice, it is taking every invoice line separately, so it rounds those amounts to -5.35 and -0.39. Then Telema is calculating total net amount based on invoice lines and gets -45.43 for coding. However the net amount in the invoice header is taken directly from the invoice and is -45.42, so Telema automatically adds rounding to the coding +0.01. 

After that invoice goes to Workaday, and in case of Credits there is next problem. In Telema amounts of credit invoices are coded with minus sign “-”. However, in Workday coding lines for credits are with +. In case of this invoice, Workday marks it as an credit note and removes minuses from coding lines, so it gets 45.43 plus rounding 0.01 = 45.44 as net amount for the credit. This is where the issue is coming from.

From my side I also notice and fix it regularly in Telema before sending invoices to WD. However, most of the invoices are automatically coded and sent to approval flow in Telema, so they don’t even reach me, but go straight to WD after approval. And for the approvers it is hard to notice this, since rounding line is added by Telema only after the invoice is fully approved and is being sent to ERP. Before that you only see small warning  about auto-corrected discrepancy as is shown on the screenshot (and of course the discrepancy itself in net amounts if you look for it)

With debit invoices and tax issues it is also coming from the original invoice. Sometimes suppliers round the tax incorrectly, or too much, and then Telema get different tax when calculating it and there is a mismatch. From Telema side I can’t change the calculated tax as it is possible in WD.

_If the Goods contain medicinal products_ -_within the meaning of the Pharmaceutical Law Act of September 6, 2001_-_, the Delivery Partner is required to place the shipment previously packed by the Partner in a separate space of a thermal insulation bag, without adding or removing any packaging, in order to ensure that Goods containing medicinal products: (i) are delivered in conditions that protect medicinal products from organic contamination and mechanical damage, as well as from microorganisms and pests, (ii) are not mixed with other Goods, (iii) are not contaminated, (iv) are transported under the temperature conditions specified for the medicinal product by the responsible entity or the relevant pharmacopoeia. Hi [~accountid:610a6c97ec92ab0070d4d852] 👋 

{panel:bgColor=#ffebe6}
*Bottom line:*

# At present, *candidate identifiers (emails, names, etc.) cannot lawfully be used* for LinkedIn lookalike audience matching.
# Why: Bolt’s current _Recruitment Privacy Notice_ does not authorise using candidate data for marketing or employer-branding purposes, and this [LinkedIn’s functionality|https://www.linkedin.com/help/lms/answer/a1489764?hcppcid=search#:~:text=generate%20your%20audience.-,Match%20your%20list%20to%20LinkedIn%20member%20accounts,-To%20match%20your] requires personal identifiers to work.
# However, if you would like to proceed “as is”, the risks would be low.
{panel}

----

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
h3. *What we can do*

# *Proceed after updating the Candidate Privacy Notice*
Once the notice explicitly includes the use of candidate data for marketing purposes such as this, the activity can lawfully go ahead with the *persona data of new candidates* - those who encounter the updated privacy notice.
# *Use anonymised recruitment statistics instead*
From my information, LinkedIn Campaign Manager can still be used by relying on *aggregated recruitment data* (e.g., job role mix, seniority, location, education background) to design targeting criteria — no personal identifiers are transferred, making this *fully compliant*.
{panel}

----

h3. 

*Context and detailed explanation*

# *Current legal position*
The existing privacy notice permits processing of candidate data only for recruitment-related purposes such as assessing suitability, preparing contracts, and fulfilling legal obligations. Marketing or employer-branding uses fall outside these purposes.
# *LinkedIn functionality*
LinkedIn’s [Matched Audiences|https://www.linkedin.com/help/lms/answer/a1489764?hcppcid=search#:~:text=generate%20your%20audience.-,Match%20your%20list%20to%20LinkedIn%20member%20accounts,-To%20match%20your] feature explicitly requires *personal identifiers* - such as names, email addresses, or device IDs - to match uploaded data with member accounts.
While identifiers are hashed locally in the browser, LinkedIn applies the same hashing method on its own data to find matches. Because those coded values can still be linked back to real individuals, this is pseudonymised, not anonymised, and therefore still personal data under GDPR.
# *Risk and compliance assessment*
The activity is *low-impact and low-risk*, given that:
#* Only basic identifiers are used (no sensitive or special category data).
#* The outcome is non-intrusive — candidates or similar profiles may see a general Bolt recruitment ad, nothing targeted or personalised.
However, without an updated lawful basis and transparency through the privacy notice, it remains technically non-compliant.
#* According to LinkedIn’s process, uploaded data is hashed locally, used solely for matching, and then deleted after processing.

h3. *Background and Regulatory Context*

Over the past years, Bolt has faced *increasing regulatory scrutiny* over its reliance on implied or soft opt-in mechanisms for direct marketing. Several markets have already escalated these concerns, and further enforcement action is likely if compliance gaps remain unaddressed.

* *Estonia (2024):*
AKI (local data protection authority) challenged Bolt’s consent mechanism, insisting on explicit opt-in consent. The Privacy team successfully deescalated the issue, but similar claims could re-emerge.
* *Poland (2023–2025):*
After 2 years of litigation, the local regulator issued a *formal warning* following privacy’s deescalation efforts. Hard opt-in remains *unimplemented*, representing a *critical compliance gap* with a high risk of fines or renewed investigation if not resolved.
* *Georgia (2025):*
Enforcement by local regulator led to a *mandatory implementation of hard opt-in consent*, now in progress. Privacy’s deescalation efforts allowed to minimise the amount of fine Bolt received for the infringement.
* *Other High-Risk Markets:*
Newer markets (e.g., *UAE, Vietnam, Italy*) show similar regulatory expectations. The risk of sudden enforcement requiring immediate hard opt-in functionality is *high and growing*.

----

h3. *Rationale and Urgency*

Implementing hard opt-in functionality is a *proactive compliance measure* to mitigate regulatory risk and protect Bolt from potential fines, enforcement actions, and reputational harm.

Failure to act exposes Bolt to:

* Immediate risk in Poland and other jurisdictions with strict consent regimes.
* Compounded operational and legal costs if emergency retrofits are required following regulatory orders.

Main code Order Data:



{noformat}df_order_data = spark.sql(
    """
with business_orders as 
(select *, 
    (bb_total_fee_sum - targeted_bonus) as profit_proxy -- why it works? because targeted_bonus in this calc includes other discounts like surcharge protect & 
from
        (
        select *,
            gmv_price_diff - COALESCE(voucher_price, 0) as targeted_bonus -- discount minus voucher discount gives targeted bonus (also includes company specific discounts like price_config)
        from
        (
            select 
                order_id,
                user_id,
                entity_id,
                ebpom.city_id,
                order_created_local_date,
                gmv_eur,
                gmv_eur_without_service_fee,
                price_eur_without_service_fee,
                service_fee,
                total_fee_sum,
                -- targeted_bonus as targeted_bonus_with_voucher,
                -- total_fee_sum+service_fee-targeted_bonus as profit_proxy, -- old wrong calculation with targeted_bonus 
                GREATEST(ebpom.gmv_eur_without_service_fee - ebpom.price_eur_without_service_fee, 0) AS gmv_price_diff, -- shows all discounts (gmv - price user paid)
                -- voucher_price, -- can't use voucher price because shows in wrong currency 
                ROUND(ebpom.voucher_price / currency.rate, 4) AS voucher_price, -- voucher price with corrected exchange rate 
                (ebpom.service_fee + ebpom.total_fee_sum) AS bb_total_fee_sum, -- for profit calculation
                --ebpom.gmv_eur_without_service_fee as gmv_eur 
                    case when is_portal then 'TA' when is_wp then 'WP' else null end wp_ta, 
                    case when product='team account - new portal'  or product='team account - old portal' or product='work profile' or product='ridebooker - cash' or product='cash ridebooker - API' or product='ridebooker - team account' or  product='ridebooker - old portal' or product='team account - API' or product='team account - voucher' or product='business delivery' or product='ridebooker - delivery' then 'RH'
                        when product='rental - business' or  product='rental - wp' then 'Rental'
                        when product='carsharing - business' or product='carsharing - wp' or product='carsharing - long term rental' then 'Carsharing'
                        when product='business food'  then 'Food' 
                    end as vertical
                from ng_public_spark.etl_business_product_order_metrics as ebpom
                /* Exchange rate join path (company → city → country → currency → rate on order date) */
                LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.etl_business_business_company AS bbc
                ON ebpom.entity_id = bbc.id
                LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_city AS company_city
                ON company_city.id = bbc.city_id
                LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country AS company_country
                ON company_country.code = company_city.country_code
                LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.currency_exchange_rates AS currency
                ON company_country.currency = currency.currency
                AND ebpom.order_created_local_date = currency.valid_on

                where ebpom.finished_orders = 1
                and ebpom.order_created_local_date >= date('{0}') and ebpom.order_created_local_date <= date('{1}')
        ) 
        )
)
  select *
  from business_orders
  where wp_ta='TA' and vertical='RH'
""".format(start,end)
).toPandas()
{noformat}

👋 Hey there!
If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

1. Open the **Client page in Admin**: [link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients?tz=Europe%2FTallinn&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D].
2. Enter the Fleet or Driver ID in the **External ID** filter field.
3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the **Invoice tasks** tab.
   * If you see *Invoice sum too small*, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Best regards,

Started iterating on the model for the first time. The existing, legacy model has a number of shortcomings:

* Not all data is used for training (only a single discount level, e.g. 30% is used as “treatment” to model the uplift, other levels then interpolated based on average treatment effects)
* Average treatment effects (to be more precise their point estimates) do not always fall on a convex hull. Because of interpolation, this propagates to CATE (individual treatment effects). Therefore, some discounts are excluded at serve time, which limits the power of discount allocation. 

There is no off-the-shelf model that solves these problems and I had to come up with a custom model – a neural network dubbed {{UpliftNet}}. In 2025W42, I have:

* Designed the architecture of the model
* Coded it up in Pytorch
** [Data preprocessing module|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/files/1079440591714199?o=3829506390716583]
** [Conversion estimator module|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/files/1079440591714335?o=3829506390716583]
** [Model trainer module|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/files/2585289337867331?o=3829506390716583]
* I have started testing the model against the baseline for the individual markets. Overall result so far:
** Better conversion ROC AUC by 1-2%
** Better Qini coefficient by ~ 2%
* Next week: understand how to put pricing into the model (which currently assumes the same ASP for all rides)

The underlying issue with “too many calls” comes from how users are “authenticated” for route-sharing. Basically users use hash for the ride as password and that’s all the authentication there is. So, from backend perspective all users who open the same link are treated as a single user.

E.g. if someone sends a tracking link to a group chat it’s possible 10 people open it and start tracking the ride. All these requests are subject to the same rate limiting constraints and can cause situations with “too many requests” responded to random people.

To properly fix it we would need to alter the way authentication works so that each person could get their own authentication fingerprint which could be used to limit excessive requests.

Hi [~accountid:712020:8bcb68bd-f8da-4da1-8320-2536f6bb0c0c] Has this contract been reviewed from the perspective of Norwegian commercial law? I can see a few provisions that seem questionable.

# Incentives (sometimes called rewards) and
# Appendix 2 saying that Bolt will promote Stella’s services and provides them data without consideration

If we agree to provide smth free of charge, them I wouldn’t expect any incentives.

Additionally, Stella will give free kWhs to the drivers based on Bolt recommendations/directions, therefore commercial link is there. Bolt will have impact on Stella’s decision. For me it looks more like a barter rather than pure partnership agreement.

The *mere signing* of a partnership agreement — meaning a document establishing cooperation or profit-sharing — *is not a taxable transaction for VAT purposes*.
 VAT applies *only to supplies of goods or services for consideration* So, if the partnership agreement only defines how parties will collaborate, share profits, or contribute resources — and there is *no payment for a specific service or supply* — then *no VAT* is due.

If the payments under the partnership agreement are *consideration for services actually performed by the partner*, those payments will normally be taxable supplies subject to VAT. If the payments are purely gratuitous (no service or other consideration), there is no VAT.

Norway defines taxable turnover as delivery of goods and services for consideration and prescribes VAT on such transactions. The starting point for any VAT analysis is whether there is a supply for consideration. In our case - no such consideration. Case could be closed. It would be even ok to have those free Kwhs from Stella treated as gratuitous. However, in Annex 2, it is mentioned that Bolt will give them drivers’ data and marketing services.

I believe we need the expert of NO commercial law because it may be perceived as a hidden barter. Bolt gives to Stella drivers’ data and marketing services in exchange for free Kwhs. Where a third party performs services that benefit the payer (e.g. promotion, marketing, sales-support) and receives payment tied to that performance, that payment is treated as consideration for a taxable service, therefore our contract may be perceived as taxable. I am not sure that just mentioning that the service will be provided free of charge protects us from being treated as a part of barter transaction. Especially that in 2.1 it is stated that: “_Under these Terms Bolt provides to the Partner Bolt Rewards Program visibility services, where Bolt Rewards Programs are showcased to Drivers using Bolt App_”.

On the other hand, appendix 2 describes the incentives as “rewards”. This narrative could help us to treat the exchange between Stella and Bolt outside of the scope of VAT but I would seek the confirmation from lawyers if this position could be easily challenged by TAs seeking the hidden barter transaction. Especially that Appendix 2 point 2.14 also gives the possibility to invoice us in very specific circumstances.

So if it were only about providing discounted EV charging services to Drivers and Fleet Owners in Norway, thereby promoting the adoption of EVs and supporting sustainable urban mobility to Drivers and FO it wouldn’t be the problem - appendix 1 p. 1 says without financial compensation. In this same point, Stella offers Bolt free kilowatt hours as incentive rewards for onboarding new FO to the Stella Platform and the aggregate consumption of qualified FO on the Stella Network. But Bolt also receives free KWhs, so it may be perceived as the remuneration for the access to the customers database (drivers).

The ways how TAs may look at this agreement: incentive paid to a business partner

* If the incentive reward is given *for achieving sales targets or promoting products*, it’s usually treated as *consideration for a service*.
* VAT applies, because the recipient provides a *marketing or promotional service* in return for payment.

Bolt will be obliged to promote Stella’s programme and share drivers data *without consideration*. Even though we will have impact on Stella’s decisions (Appendix 2 point 1.1 I_n coordination with the Partner, Bolt can instruct the Partner to credit the Reward Kilowatt Hours to Fleet Owners to incentivise engagement on the Bolt Platform and drive desired behaviours)_

*Direct link:* Payment (free Kwhs) is directly linked to a specific activity/performance (promotion, data sharing). 

*Expectation:* Bolt is expected/contractually obliged to deliver customers to Stella- see Annex 4.14

*Documented in contract:* There is a written contract describing the service. Here we are covered by mentioning that all the undertakings are free of charge, but does it protect us enough? 

Therefore I believe that those doubts shall be raised to lawyers to seek their confirmation that current wording of the PA is strong enough to reject any attempts of seeking the barter between Bolt and Stella.

Hi! The reason for the difference between what driver saw and what admin shows afterwards is that when the work time suspension starts, it is actually scheduled to be 12 hours longer than necessary. It is ended at the correct time by the system later, but the driver does see an incorrect time because of it.

This 12 hour buffer is needed because a driver is allowed to finish their last order even if they are already suspended due to reaching work time limit. Since that order can, in rare cases, be many hours long, the suspension tries to cover for that. It is made shorter later when the driver actually has rested enough.

Due to this issue showing actual end time of the block to the driver is incorrect in that case because the end time is always further in the future than it needs to be while the driver is suspended.

I will have to return to this issue later. Below are some technical notes to continue.

Because of the "last order" issue, it is not possible to avoid changes to the end of work time limit suspensions - having an active order when driver reaches the limit will extend the suspension by the time they went over the limit. Improvements to the suspension logic can approach this in two ways:

1. Keep displaying actual end time of the suspension. Keep suspensions longer than needed initially, but update the end time as soon as driver state changes. There will be a small gap immediately after driver goes offline when they will still see the incorrect block time if they try to go online immediately after getting pushed offline.
2. Keep displaying actual end time. Keep updating the block end time while the driver is still online after reaching the time limit. The driver will still see somewhat incorrect time if they try to go online immediately after being pushed offline, but that will be much closer to the actual expected end time.
3. Do not show real suspension end time. Instead for work time block calculate the expected time they may go online according to the configuration if it is earlier than the actual block end time. The reason why it is acceptable to do so is that if the driver can see the suspension message, that means that they are actually offline. This means that even if we did not handle the driver state change yet on our side. We can either try to get driver state history to get the correct time when they went offline, or instead get a "close enough" time by using current time (in which case we need to implement either 1 or 2 so that the visible end time does not keep slipping further and further). Another issue is that there is no particularly good place to technically implement this logic special to the work time suspension so that it show up consistently both to drivers and ops.
This seems like a fairly large change, whichever way we approach it.
I think previously we tried to hide the end time from the suspension screen for that reason, but this was obviously sub-optimal as well.

** Before painting, how is the vehicle cleaned? For paint to stick properly, there shouldn’t be any dust/dirt/oil/silicone residue as it will result in the coat not sticking & paint coming off later.
** How is the masking done for everything else which is not covered by the jigs?
* *3D printed masking jigs*
** Looking at the images, the coverage of the jigs is not very accurate. As a result, there is a lot of overspray on different parts which should not get paint on them:
*** Rear wheel/mudguard cover jig - the rear mudguard has a lot of overspray on the rear dropout area - that looks quite bad and leaves an unprofessional impression. IMO the jig does not fulfill its purpose if there is so much overspray.
*** Front wheel cover jig - front wheel axle nuts & brake fixation bolt are covered under a heavy coat of paint. This will have an impact on maintenance and during that, manipulating these fasteners will chip off the paint around it. This looks bad and is also not sustainable for maintenance, it shouldn’t be painted over! There is also overspray on the front mudguard, so I would say again that the jig is not fulfilling its purpose.
*** Charging adapter jig - no comments, as no visual evidence as to how well it works.
* *Top area masking*
** It looks like it is very simplistically done, as long as all non-paintable parts are covered, then fine.
* *Non-masked/undocumented parts*
** It is not described how the underside of the scooter gets covered/painted - is the controller compartment cover & bolts just painted over?
** It is not described how the VIN code/QR and regulatory/info labels are conserved during painting procedure
** It is not described how the Bolt logo gets covered/painted over/reapplied.
** It is not described how the bag hook gets covered.
** It is not described how the reflectors/uncovered grip tapes get masked.
** It is not described how the battery compartment is left during painting. It is vital that the compartment is sealed!
** It is not described how the charging port is covered - one one picture it looks like it was just painted over.
* *Painting quality*
** The “test-paint” unit looks like it has plenty of overspray, aforementioned areas painted over (which were described that they shouldn’t be painted over) and the general finish lacks gloss and looks like it has been aerosol-sprayed. This would suggest that the painting setup is not well configured (Insufficient paint flow, incorrectly mixed (thinned) paint, incorrect nozzle configuration etc.). The end product looks like it has been painted with a budget of 
** The vehicle does not seem too well prepared before painting - all of the imperfections (holes, grooves, chips, dents) are just painted over and still show.
** In general, if what I mentioned above is acceptable outcome for LOPS, then there are no counterarguments. Just for consideration.
* *Cost*
** There is no cost per vehicle calculated for this project, only estimate is paint required per vehicle and there is a breakdown of paint booth materials cost. There is no estimation of how much time one vehicle/set of vehicles takes to repaint, what is the preparation time, paint time, and thus the general resource cost per one vehicle repaint. As mentioned in the document itself, “…the biggest part of the process is preparing the scooter for painting.” but it is not quantified at all.

Conclusion - This is not a process documentation. Most importantly, the end result is a vehicle with a quick new layer of paint, which still looks very rough but just slightly fresher. There is a lot of overspray which makes the finish of the scooter look cheap. If the cost per unit is very low, effort is low and the outcome is acceptable for management, then it is up to you. 

The biggest concern for HW team is the safety/regulatory part and repercussions, as we know based on the Bucharest example (DIY paint booth) that the situation resolved with a lot of problems in the end.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt is having a Halloween giveaway in the UK, with the prize being £100 Amazon vouchers ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/GDEAZHCUV/p1761149079833109]).
** Period is between 27 October (today) and 2 November. Unfortunately, Olabowale Musa only looped me in at 9am today :melting_face: 
** If a driver completes 2 scheduled rides during this period, they will be eligible. 5 drivers selected randomly.
* Giveaway will be promoted via email comms / push notifications ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1VyfcS9fGF3TGrDd67sjpRkTpeHyyBo_Tlo51trqWKME/edit?tab=t.0]). There will also be an in-app message sent out.
** Winners will be contacted by telephone or email.
* There is also a separate campaign in tandem whereby FB drivers who comment ‘Halloween’ on a post ([link|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cWpHKvPyBqO0fsbz8ditx8si8x0R7m3scP0lAhM3x6M/edit?slide=id.g386414429b5_0_0#slide=id.g386414429b5_0_0]) (and who have completed 2 SRs) will be entered into the draw. 
* Winners will be announced via an in-app message.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* General:
** Privacy notice covers the envisaged processing activity.
** Presumably we are just looking at scheduled ride completion status, so the eligibility processing does not look invasive.
** We can rely on soft opt-in here, so no need for consent to receive the comms.
** Since the campaign is {color:#36b37e}*low-risk*{color}, it also does not matter that it is automatic enrolment,
* T&CS ([link|https://sites.google.com/bolt.eu/bolt-gb/gb-drivers-scheduled-rides-amazon-vouchers-giveaway] - see Clause 7):
** Eligibility criteria are clear, and so it is obvious what personal data will be processed here ✅ 
** Links to the correct driver privacy notice ✅ 
** By accepting the prize, the winner consents to their details being published online and via marketing channels - this is not an ideal legal basis ⚠️ 
*** Legitimate interest, rather than contractual necessity, is more likely to be applicable as a legal basis here, due to the potentially widespread nature of the publicity. As such, the winner must be given the opportunity to opt-out.
*** To play it safe (given the limited review time available), we can rely on both (i.e., leave it ambiguous). Amend Clause 7.2 to the following: “_By accepting the Prize, Winners_ +*_agree_*+ _to the Giveaways Terms and Conditions._ +*_Winners acknowledge that Bolt will publish or make_*+ _available his/her name, likeness, image and/or voice (including photograph and video recording of the same) and country in Bolt’s website and any other marketing channels, including social media channels and newsletters,_ +*_as necessary to fulfill the these Special Terms and Conditions_*+_._ +*_Alternatively, in jurisdictions where consent is the only lawful basis for processing, we will rely on the Winner’s consent._*+ _Bolt may be required to provide the Winner’s information and winning entry to a regulatory authority on request. It is a condition of accepting the Prize that a Winner may be required to sign a legal release in a form to be determined by Bolt in its absolute discretion._”
*** Clause 7.3 can be left as is. Amend Clause 7.4 to the following: “_If you object to any or all of your_ +*_name_*+_, country and winning entry being published or made available, please contact us by emailing_ [_giveaways.uk@bolt.eu_|mailto:giveaways.uk@bolt.eu]_,_ +*_and such request will be considered in accordance with applicable requirements_*+_. Bolt must still provide the information and winning entry to the Advertising Standards Authority on request_.”
* Comms:
** Email / Push / Inbox ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1VyfcS9fGF3TGrDd67sjpRkTpeHyyBo_Tlo51trqWKME/edit?tab=t.0]):
*** Should contain a link to the T&Cs ⚠️ 
** FB ([link|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1cWpHKvPyBqO0fsbz8ditx8si8x0R7m3scP0lAhM3x6M/edit?slide=id.g386414429b5_0_0#slide=id.g386414429b5_0_0]):
*** No comments. Links to T&Cs, so fine ✅ 
* Winner announcement:
** Ideally, we should not over-share information about the winner here. For example, first name only ⚠️ 
** Given the time available, it seems unlikely that we will be able to collect separate consent to publication. As such, we will need to rely on an alternative legal basis (e.g., contractual necessity / legitimate interest). Given that this giveaway is low risk, this should be ok.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Advice:
** Edit the T&Cs per the comments above.
** Clarify exactly what data we will be publishing online / in channels (ensure it is minimal), and adapt Clause 7 accordingly.
** Ensure a link to the T&Cs is contained in all comms.
** Ensure that Privacy Team are looped in sooner next time.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

The summary from the top 10 DBT jobs optimization:

# Photon usage & sizing
Many presets use Photon by default. Photon have a higher DBU rate (≈2–3× on AWS Jobs, depends on SKU). It’s great for CPU-bound SQL/DataFrame workloads (joins/aggregations). If a pipeline is shuffle-bound or skewed, fix those first—Photon won’t remove network/disk contention. When enabling Photon, start by reducing cores/instances ~40–50% vs. your non-Photon baseline and re-benchmark time vs. cost (DBUs × hours).
# Driver sizing
Large drivers are rarely needed; the driver mostly coordinates work. In only a few cases did a very large driver help; otherwise it wasted money. Default to a modest driver (e.g., {{mgd-fleet.2xlarge}} or {{rgd-fleet.2xlarge}}; often even {{xlarge}} is fine). Scale the driver up only if the Spark UI shows driver pressure (high CPU/GC, scheduler backlog, OOM).
# Instance choice, Spot strategy & availability
For short jobs (≤1–2h), general-purpose families are fine. For long-running jobs, avoid Spot-only: keep the driver on On-Demand and diversify Spot workers across instance types and AZs with capacity-optimized (or price-capacity-optimized) allocation. Use [this|https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/spot/instance-advisor/] AWS Spot availability website for more information regarding availability.
# Shuffle-heavy jobs: fewer, larger workers + fast local disks
For heavy joins/aggregations (big shuffles), prefer fewer, larger workers with locally attached NVMe (e.g., *d families: m6id/c6id/r6id). This reduces network and disk I/O during shuffle. Rely on AQE first; 
# Avoid oversized workers
We observed 16xlarge/24xlarge workers <50% utilized. Start from 2xlarge/4xlarge, then iterate based on CPU, memory, spilled bytes, and shuffle read/write in the Spark UI. Generally 2x-4x would be enough.
# Skew & long-tail tasks
“99 tasks finish fast, 1 runs 30–40 min” is almost always skew. In that case the optimization could be only done in code. So for such cases it is usually not recommended to enable photon, since it will waste quite a lot of money on the same shuffling, but it worth to try if the job is not long running.
# Code/modeling (dbt)
Besides the recommendations for infrastructure configuration, the root cause of slow jobs are almost always in inefficient code. There are a lot of huge jobs which are using {{insert overwrite}} instead of incremental update and load the data for 2 to 15 years, which is super huge and inefficient. Using at least the incremental updates where possible could completely eliminate the need for cluster optimization. Before that cluster changes could help till it is done.

Next steps, we could start changing the existing presets in according to the recommendations, but checking the metrics for the jobs before. We could start from specific modules like {{central-ops}} and see the overall stability of those.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Marten

Hi [~accountid:610a6c97ec92ab0070d4d852] 👋

{panel:bgColor=#ffebe6}
*Bottom line:*

# At present, *candidate identifiers (emails, names, etc.) cannot lawfully be used* for LinkedIn lookalike audience matching.
# *Why*:
## Bolt’s current _Recruitment Privacy Notice_ does not authorise using candidate data for marketing or employer-branding purposes
## this [+LinkedIn’s functionality+|https://www.linkedin.com/help/lms/answer/a1489764?hcppcid=search#:~:text=generate%20your%20audience.-,Match%20your%20list%20to%20LinkedIn%20member%20accounts,-To%20match%20your] *requires personal identifiers to work* (details why under “Context and detailed explanation”.
# However, if you would like to proceed “as is”, the risks would be low.
{panel}

----

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
h3. *What we can do*

# *Proceed after updating the Candidate Privacy Notice*
Once the notice explicitly includes the use of candidate data for marketing purposes such as this, the activity can lawfully go ahead with the *persona data of new candidates* - those who encounter the updated privacy notice.
# *Use anonymised recruitment statistics instead*
From my information, LinkedIn Campaign Manager can still be used by relying on *aggregated recruitment data* (e.g., job role mix, seniority, location, education background) to design targeting criteria — no personal identifiers are transferred, making this *fully compliant*.
{panel}

----

h3. 

*Context and detailed explanation*

# *Current legal position*
The existing privacy notice permits processing of candidate data only for recruitment-related purposes such as assessing suitability, preparing contracts, and fulfilling legal obligations. Marketing or employer-branding uses fall outside these purposes.
# *LinkedIn functionality*
LinkedIn’s [+Matched Audiences+|https://www.linkedin.com/help/lms/answer/a1489764?hcppcid=search#:~:text=generate%20your%20audience.-,Match%20your%20list%20to%20LinkedIn%20member%20accounts,-To%20match%20your] feature explicitly requires *personal identifiers* - such as names, email addresses, or device IDs - to match uploaded data with member accounts.
While identifiers are hashed locally in the browser, LinkedIn applies the same hashing method on its own data to find matches. Because those coded values can still be linked back to real individuals, this is pseudonymised, not anonymised, and therefore still personal data under GDPR.
# *Risk and compliance assessment*
The activity is *low-impact and low-risk*, given that:
#* Only basic identifiers are used (no sensitive or special category data).
#* The outcome is non-intrusive — candidates or similar profiles may see a general Bolt recruitment ad, nothing targeted or personalised.
However, without an updated lawful basis and transparency through the privacy notice, it remains technically non-compliant.
#* According to LinkedIn’s process, uploaded data is hashed locally, used solely for matching, and then deleted after processing.

Based on my review of the document, Bolt (Customer) has several key obligations related to card issuing:

# *Platform and User Interface Obligations:*

1.1. Customer must build, operate, and maintain the User Interface in accordance with the applicable Regional Supplements.

1.2. Customer must enable the Connected Accounts to access the Connected Account Services via the User Interface by providing User Access Management Services

# *Onboarding and KYC:*

2.1. Customer will facilitate Airwallex's onboarding process by creating an onboarding flow within the User Interface ("Onboarding Flow").

2.2. Customer must collect Onboarding Data from Connected Accounts and pass the Onboarding Data to Airwallex through the API within due time

# *Support and Customer Service:*

3.1. Customer must provide Connected Account Support Services to Airwallex and acknowledges that it will be the first point of contact for the Connected Accounts for any query regarding the Embedded Finance Solution

# *Marketing and disclosures:*

4.1. Customer {color:#bf2600}*must obtain Airwallex's prior written approval for Marketing Materials*{color} relating to the Embedded Finance Solution, which must be sent at least fifteen (15) Business Days before publication

4.2. Customer must accurately describe the Embedded Finance Solution and will not misrepresent any feature

4.3. Customer {color:#bf2600}*must not hold itself out as the provider of the Connected Account Services*{color}

# *Billing and Fee Collection:*

5.1. For Customer and Connected Account Usage: This fee will be charged to the Lead Customer Entity (Bolt Operations OU). Customer acknowledges and agrees that Airwallex may debit this fee from Customer's Wallet (Connected Account). 

# *Legal and compliance:*

6.1. Customer shall provide the Platform Services in compliance with Applicable Law and {color:#bf2600}*is fully responsible for any tax or legal assessment relating to the Platform Fees*{color}.



I understand no other agreement/addendum is needed for this product. However,  the MSA doesn't specify additional card-specific obligations beyond these general Embedded Finance Solution requirements that would apply to {color:#bf2600}*all products including card issuing*{color}.

Hi, Ernests! Sorry for the long wait.

This is not a London driver, so the PHV/PHL check should not run for that profile at all. It is not the question of having correct documents - we should not check them against TfL for drivers outside London.

This is caused by two separate issues:

• We do not correctly update city ID when copying *manual* suspensions as part of driver copy. In this case a driver with a London profile had a custom suspension when the driver profile was copied to a different city. The copy of the block retained London city ID. You can find that suspension under "past suspensions", ID 90760624, though nothing will really tell you that it is a "London" suspension. When that suspension was cancelled, this caused the event to be sent as if that was a block of a London driver.
• The logic in the PHV/PHL checks trusts the city ID in the block events it receives. In this case it received an event that the custom suspension was cancelled, and treated the driver as if they were a London driver. It did not find correct London documents (as expected, since, again, this is not actually a London driver profile) and suspended the driver.
When PHV/PHL documents were added later, they were treated "correctly" in the sense that London document checks were completely skipped as this is not a London driver. Sadly in this case this meant that the driver was left suspended.

Both issues need to be fixed. For driver manual suspension copy this means adding updating target city ID. For London checks it means actually checking driver city ID instead of relying on the event city ID.

It is a bit more tricky to find incorrect suspensions caused by those issues. I think we need two separate passes:
• Find any suspensions inconsistent with entity city and update city ID on them to prevent this from happening further.
    ◦ This is a cross-service query for data warehouse. As a simplification to run within block DB, we can look for any entity with suspensions from different cities, as that is a clear sign of this issue. This might miss cases when the entity has _only_ incorrectly copied suspensions.
• Find any PHV/PHL check suspensions outside London and cancel them, as they will never be cancelled automatically.
I will be working further on fixing this.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Bolt Business ‘Commission Tier’ Definitions below (Tier = T):

* *T0:* 3000+ orders or GMV ≥ 3000 × ASP within 90 consecutive days. Projection applies for <90 days.
* *T1:* 700+ orders or GMV ≥ 700 × ASP within 90 days. Projection applies for <90 days.
* *T2:* 250+ orders or GMV ≥ 250 × ASP within 90 days. Projection applies for <90 days.
* *T3:* 30+ orders or GMV ≥ 30 × ASP within 90 days. Projection applies for <90 days.
* *T4*: 1+ orders or GMV ≥ 1 × ASP within 90 days. Projection applies for <90 days.

*For companies operating <90 days, a linear projection based on average daily orders and GMV applies.
** Important: All tiers in this dashboard follow the Commission Tier Definitions, Group Accounts are tiered as one combined account.
*** Rollover GMV: GMV of current quarter ride from companies with first riding date in the previous quarter.
**** Eligible GMV = GMV from companies with first riding date in this quarter + Rollover GMV

To summarise - T0 clients are the most important to us. T3 and and T4 get the most minimal amount of attention from a business point of view.

Dear Ersan,

Thank you for reaching out and for taking the time to share your experience with us.

According to our records, you were driving under the fleet COR FORTIUM j.d.o.o., which is an independent transport operator using the Bolt platform. This means that all drivers engaged through that fleet are employed or contracted by the fleet directly, not by Bolt. Bolt’s role is limited to providing the technological platform and facilitating trip payments between passengers and licensed transport operators.

Under Croatian law, ride-hailing platforms like Bolt and Uber operate under the same legal framework — neither company directly employs drivers. Instead, drivers provide services through licensed transport companies (fleets) that choose to use a given platform. When you mention that you are now “working directly with Uber,” this almost certainly means you are driving for another fleet that cooperates with Uber in the same way your previous fleet cooperated with Bolt.

We fully understand your frustration regarding non-payment. However, as your contractual relationship was with COR FORTIUM j.d.o.o., that company is solely responsible for salary payments and other employment-related obligations. Bolt does not have the legal authority to intervene in such disputes or access details of individual payments between fleets and their drivers.

If your former employer has failed to pay you, we recommend addressing the matter directly with them.

We sincerely regret the difficulties you have faced and appreciate that you shared your concerns with us. Please be assured that Bolt continuously reviews the reliability and compliance of its partner fleets to ensure fair and lawful cooperation across the platform.

Kind regards,

h2. Okta Apps

We’ve identified all the apps integrated with Okta. They can be found in [this doc|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1936fa_hTdvo8PdXbklYF15ekc8kpj8UzHv96KuijKOs/edit?usp=sharing].

*The Good News*

* The majority of apps use *SSO* (via *SAML* or *OIDC*).
* Several also have *SCIM* enabled.
** If the *Features* column includes {{PUSH_USER_DEACTIVATION}}, it means that when a user is deactivated in Okta, they’re also automatically deactivated in that app.

*The Not-So-Good News*

* A few apps don’t support SSO, specifically those with *Sign On Mode: BOOKMARK*.
* For these, when an account is terminated:
** Our {{okta}} bolt-server service automatically creates an *SD ticket* for IT Support to manually deactivate the user in that app.
** However, this only happens *if* the app is included in the [whitelist|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/dynamic-config/entity/edit/b2t0YS9va3RhX2FwcGxpY2F0aW9uX3NlcnZpY2Uvb2t0YV9ib29rbWFya19hcHBsaWNhdGlvbl93aGl0ZWxpc3Q=/:shard].
** If it’s *not whitelisted*, the user’s account remains active in that app.

*Next Steps*

* As a follow-up action, we’ll update the logic of the {{okta}} service to create a _termination_ ticket for all Okta apps that don’t have SSO enabled and don’t automatically deactivate a user's account. 
** Follow-up ticket: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/PAW-12852|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/PAW-12852|smart-link]

In addition, we have included an explanatory clarification of the activities of a debt collection company regarding the GDPR (as follows) and hope that this will provide clarity on the classification of our debt collection activities:_

_Based on Document No. 16 of the_ [*_German Data Protection Conference (DSK)_*|https://www.datenschutzkonferenz-online.de/media/kp/dsk_kpnr_16.pdf]_, the provision of receivables management services does NOT constitute jointly determined use of data according to Art. 26 GDPR nor processing according to Art. 28 GDPR. Rather, the use of data is necessary to be able to provide the contractual receivables management service in all its forms. The customer has a duty to cooperate in providing the necessary personal data in order to successfully perform this service. There is no ‘jointly determination’ on the purposes and means of processing according to Art. 26 GDPR, as this would require each of the parties involved to have a decisive actual influence on the data processing, which is not the case in view of the regulations in the competence framework._

_Joint controllers must be distinguished in particular from contract processing pursuant to Art. 28 GDPR and from the transfer of personal data to a controller according to Art. 4 No. 7 GDPR where the parties involved do not jointly determine the purposes and means of processing. Examples of joint processing include Facebook fan page = joint responsibility between Facebook and the operators of the Facebook fan page or, for example, a joint research and development platform._

_The fact that all parties involved have an economic interest in the processing is not in itself sufficient to establish joint responsibility according to Art. 26 GDPR. Service providers who merely provide processing services for a fee naturally have an economic interest in this, but as long as they do not jointly determine means and purposes, they are not jointly responsible._

_However, the provision of receivables management services does not constitute a) order processing or b) joint processing of data._

Hi [~accountid:712020:79bdda29-2f20-4318-9d05-92c9d0bd7b47] This was one time deal that carried some risks that the business accepted:

Under Article 33(1) of the Croatian VAT Act and Article 73 of the EU VAT Directive (2006/112/EC), any exchange of goods or services for consideration is taxable, even if consideration is in kind rather than monetary.

If the agreement defines reciprocal promotional deliverables (e.g. “Bolt shall promote HNK on its app; HNK shall promote Bolt in its materials”), the Tax Administration may interpret it as a taxable barter transaction.

* Each side would then be obliged to issue an invoice for the market value of the service provided and account for VAT.
* This can trigger penalties or back-assessed VAT if the transaction is later audited.


We could mitigate these risks by avoid language implying reciprocal obligations or measurable promotional value. Instead, state that each party may independently decide to carry out promotional activities voluntarily and without commercial consideration.

Additionally, since HNK (Croatian National Theatre) is a publicly funded institution, any cooperation providing Bolt with visibility or promotional benefit could be interpreted as public procurement or state aid, depending on the form and benefit.
If the cooperation grants Bolt access to public communication channels or assets (e.g. use of HNK’s name, premises, or logo), HNK’s legal team might request a more formal contract or procurement-based justification.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

_entities related to the client (such as the parent company, subsidiary or related entities);_

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

Hi [~accountid:5d9c300987dd6f0dcb4d2b58] please find answer to your question below:

Bolt can proceed with establishing a Service Level Agreement (SLA) with Odysse under the Principal Model.

Reasoning:

* In the Principal Model, Odysse, not individual drivers, is Bolt’s contracting partner.
* Odysse employs and manages its own drivers and is responsible for meeting performance expectations.
* This means Bolt can lawfully set and monitor fleet-level KPIs (such as average online hours, acceptance rates, completion rates, congestion-zone or airport trips) as commercial terms of the fleet contract.

Key conditions to stay compliant:

* KPIs must apply to the fleet as a whole, not to individual drivers.
* Odysse must have freedom to decide how it meets the KPIs.
* Avoid any language or practice that directs, disciplines or evaluates individual drivers, as that could create worker-status or employment-law risk.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Hi [~accountid:5e4655bb691b8a0c95c27708] ,

I’ve now reviewed our Purchase Agreement with TWS taking into account the issue at hand. Below is my view on the aspects you raised, as well as a few points I’d like to confirm.

# *Replacement of Faulty Batteries*

Under the Purchase Agreement, TWS is contractually responsible for the conformity, safety, and quality of all batteries delivered to Bolt (clause 10.1). This includes components sourced from their sub-suppliers, hence, the LG cells. 

The contract explicitly makes TWS liable for “any and all damages caused to Bolt or third parties due to non-compliance with quality requirements.”

Therefore, TWS should be responsible for replacing all affected batteries and bear associated costs, regardless of LG’s involvement.

# *Replacement Outside Warranty Period*

I agree with you. If the batteries are faulty from day one, TWS should be responsible for fixing them even if the warranty has expired. The written statement from LG (confirming a manufacturing fault) is critical evidence.

I assume we have written communications with TWS about the issue, but please confirm. This is key to prove Bolt’s efforts in communicating hidden defects as per clause 5.5.

# *Coverage for Future Failures*

Given that we can’t immediately identify and replace every defective unit now, we can argue that all batteries from the affected batches are non-conforming as a group. We can seek a standing replacement commitment from TWS covering any units that later exhibit the same failure.

I suggest that we push TWS to issue a written acknowledgement in the form of a letter confirming their obligation to replace any affected units throughout the lifetime of the batteries, as you suggested. Has there been any discussion with TWS along these lines yet?

# *Liability in Case of Fire or Safety Event*

You’re correct that, in any fire or safety incident, Bolt will be the first point of liability as product owner/distributor. However, the contract clearly gives us recourse against TWS. They’re liable for all damages to Bolt and third parties arising from quality non-compliance (clause 10.1).

TWS might be entitled to submit its own claims against LG depending on their arrangement. However, this should not affect TWS’s responsibilities as a supplier towards Bolt.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Hi [~accountid:618124ab3e3753006f742d1c] , summarizing my views/case below. Note that the legal basis is not valid, however, if the authority is persistent: the request is legitimate so we have an option to disclose data based on our legitimate interest, if this is something that the Bolt Food team sees fit.



* Article 75(4) of the Environment Protection Act empowers the ERA to request the assistance of the Police, Armed Forces, Transport Malta, or other competent government entities in enforcement. 
** Link: [https://legislation.mt/eli/cap/549/eng/pdf|https://legislation.mt/eli/cap/549/eng/pdf|smart-link] 
** It does not create a binding obligation for private companies such as Bolt to disclose personal data.
** Therefore, Article 6(1)(c) GDPR (legal obligation) does not apply.
* If Bolt were to share data, the correct basis would be Article 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interests) - the ERA’s legitimate interest in environmental law enforcement balanced against the customer’s privacy rights.

h3. *_Overview of data disclosure legality_*

* The purpose (investigating a specific littering incident) is legitimate and narrowly defined.
* Sharing should be limited to the minimum necessary data to identify the individual linked to order MOH75:
** We can share customer name and delivery address (to identify the individual and location of delivery).
** We should omit the phone number unless ERA demonstrates it is _strictly necessary_ for follow-up (e.g., to verify identity).
** No other data (e.g., payment details, previous orders) should be provided.

h3. *_Recommended Next Steps_*

# Respond to the ERA explaining that Article 75(4) does not legally compel Bolt to disclose personal data.
# Invite ERA to route the request through the Malta Police or another competent enforcement body empowered to compel disclosure.
# If ERA insists and Bolt decides to cooperate:
#* Share only the name and delivery address, omitting contact details unless justified.

Example of agreements signed between LHV and the dealer, and between Bolt and the dealer:

[^Buyout obligation agreement (1) (2).docx]
[^Contract of purchase and sale (1) (1).docx]
[^Dealer Buyback Agreement - - Bolt - clean 07.06.2024 (1) (2).docx]

Summary still being confirmed:

# *Contract of Purchase and Sale.* Between LHV and dealer. Dealer commits to sell the vehicles to LHV and deliver them to Bolt as the Lessee. LHV commits to buy the vehicles from the dealer and pay for them. Bolt is not a party to the contract although it provides for certain rights and obligations to Bolt (take possession of the vehicles, claim compensation for delays etc.).
# *Buyout Obligation Agreement.* Between LHV and dealer. Dealer commits to buy the vehicles back from LHV after the lease end and pay the (re)purchase price. LHV commits to prepare documentation and transfer ownership of the vehicles to dealer. Bolt is not a party to the agreement although it provides for certain rights and obligations to Bolt (transferring control of the vehicle to the dealer, participating in disputes about vehicle’s condition).
# *Dealer Buyback Agreement.* Between Bolt and dealer. Bolt can enforce the buyback obligation laid down in the Buyout obligation agreement towards the dealer (“Lessor’s Saleback Right”). Alternatively, and provided certain conditions are met, Bolt can also demand that the dealer purchases vehicles directly from Bolt (“Lessee’s Saleback Right”) for the repurchase price set out in the Dealer Buyback Agreement. Few exceptions aside (e.g., quantity limitations to the Lessee’s Saleback Right), this agreement is quite similar to the buyback agreements Bolt usually signs with Swedbank/Luminor and dealers.

There’s no separate buyback/buyout agreement between Bolt and LHV, right? At least not beforehand. There might be one if the dealer fails to fulfil the Buyout Obligation Agreement. I assume that under the lease framework Bolt is ultimately liable towards LHV for the vehicles and the buyback.

*From IBFD 27 October 2025:*

Belgium

_Report from Dr René Offermanns, IBFD Principal Associates_

*Belgium Issues Guidance on Pillar Two Rules*

The Belgian Federal Public Service (SPF) Finance has published a circular with detailed guidance on the application of the minimum tax for multinational enterprise groups and large domestic groups and the OECD Guidance until 2024. The minimum tax is based on the [+Minimum Taxation Directive (2022/2523)+|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/eulaw_2022_2523_eng__td1] (Directive), which provides for a minimum effective tax rate of 15% for groups, both domestic and international, with combined financial revenues of more than EUR 750 million a year, and with either a parent company or a subsidiary situated in an EU Member State.

The minimum tax was introduced by a separate law of 19 December 2023 and applies from 31 December 2023 (_see_ [+Belgium Enacts Law Implementing Minimum Taxation Directive (28 December 2023)+|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/tns_2023-12-28_be_1]).

The Directive guarantees an EU-wide implementation of the OECD global anti-base-erosion rules, the income inclusion rule and the undertaxed profits rule included in the OECD Pillar Two.

Based on both the Directive and the OECD rules, large MNE groups must pay additional tax in jurisdictions where their effective tax rate is below 15%. In addition, the Directive also applies to large-scale domestic groups. In line with the GLoBE rules, Belgium also has introduced a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT).

The Circular contains guidance on the definitions, scope of the tax, determination of GLoBE income, the calculation of the adjusted covered taxes, the calculation of the Effective Tax Rate (ETR) and top‑up taxes, the QDMTT; the Income Inclusion Rule (IIR), the Under-Taxed Payment Rule (UTPR), special rules concerning tax neutrality and dividend regimes, the collection of the minimum tax, the transitional rules and the effective dates.

The main clarifications of the Circular, which explains that the important parts of the Belgian Pillar Two law generally follow the OECD rules and the Directive, are summarized below.

*_QDMTT_*

The Belgian QDMTT computation differs from the jurisdictional calculation under OECD Model Rules because taxes attributed to constituent entities in Belgium from foreign permanent establishments, controlled foreign corporation regimes, hybrid entities and entities that make distribution are excluded.

In addition, it is indicated that for the domestic top-up tax, taxes paid by a Belgian constituent entity shareholder on profit or loss are not taken into account.

Those exclusions aim to simplify the calculation of the domestic top-up-tax.

*_Tax Liability_*

According to the Circular, Belgium applies group-level liability for the QDMTT and the IIR and a system of joint and several liability between the constituent entities applies.

Furthermore, if several constituent entities are established in Belgium, the top-up tax is levied on the constituent entity with the largest net income.

In this context, Belgium also provides for a tax-neutral intragroup compensation system.

*_Transitional Regime_*

Until 30 June 2027, Belgium will apply a transitional allocation method for blended CFC regimes.

*_R&D Tax Credit_*

The research and development tax credit can be repaid after four assessment years instead of five, making it a qualified repayable tax credit. Under Belgian law, this tax credit can either be offset against corporate income tax or non-resident corporate income tax or be deferred.

In addition, it is indicated that allowing in-scope groups to decide whether to allocate the R&D tax credit enables a constituent entity to defer the allocation for the year or years in which the application of the credit for the constituent entity would result in an ETR below 15%.

*_Safe Harbours_*

The circular also deals with safe harbours, including the transitional UTPR safe harbour. Last-mentioned applies to fiscal years starting before 1 January 2026 and ending before 31 December 2026.

The safe harbour rules provide that in-scope MNE groups are temporarily shielded from the UTPR if its ultimate parent entity is established in a jurisdiction with a corporate tax rate of at least 20%.

Concerning the permanent QDMTT safe harbour, it is indicated that if a jurisdiction has introduced a QDMTT, Belgium allows the filing entity to zero out the GLoBE top-up tax in that jurisdiction.

*_Effective Dates_*

The IIR and QDMTT apply to fiscal years starting on or after 31 December 2023, while the UTPR applies to fiscal years beginning on or after 31 December 2024.

The above explained R&D tax credit amendments apply from the 2025 tax year.

The full text of Circular 2025/C/68 of 22 October 2025 is available [+here+|https://www.minfin.fgov.be/myminfin-web/pages/public/fisconet/document/9564efa7-488c-4c94-82f5-b433e46c9657#_Toc208585973] (in Dutch) and [+here+|https://www.minfin.fgov.be/myminfin-web/pages/public/fisconet/document/bcb8111b-52a3-433d-90fa-f91ae7bf63af] in French.

Did some investigation and found that the slots under the lock are causing a situation where the levers of the lock might get stucked.

The slots are caused by a production method of that bracket:

* bracket is stamped with all the holes
* gas welded nuts are welded to the bracket from back side (it is not possible to control the flatness on the front side. even if the nut reaches to the front surface in the beginning then during the welding it will be heated and gets deformed and there will be surface differences)



|!image-20251028-074913.png|width=359,alt="image-20251028-074913.png"!
The spacer /supporting pipe inside the lock is fixed to the casing of the lock but the other end can move freely through the back cover of the lock. If there is a flat surface around the bolt then it will block the movement of the spacer but otherwise the spacer will be forced into the slot and it will cause a deformation inside the lock.|!image-20251028-075155.png|width=359,alt="image-20251028-075155.png"!|!image-20251028-075243.png|width=359,alt="image-20251028-075243.png"!|
|!image-20251028-075311.png|width=359,alt="image-20251028-075311.png"!
Added bigger washer around the spacer that simulates the slot on the bracket|!9a46148de2e50d6e136e8910e9d93e4e.mp4|width=359,alt="9a46148de2e50d6e136e8910e9d93e4e.mp4"!
\\
When the bolts are fixed and the supporting pipe can move into the slot the lock will get stucked|!4d33f08db764d13ac6ab5c5a6dbcaf68.mp4|width=359,alt="4d33f08db764d13ac6ab5c5a6dbcaf68.mp4"!
\\
When I removed the washer and do not let the supporting pipe to move into the slot the lock works well.|



Conclusion:

The surface under the lock must be completely flat or we may not rotate the the lock 180 degrees



{color:#ff5630}*OPTION 1*{color}

|!image-20251028-080129.png|width=359,alt="image-20251028-080129.png"!

!image-20251028-080236.png|width=359,alt="image-20251028-080236.png"!

Gas welded nuts|
